speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROCEDURE RESPECTING BILL TO AMEND THE INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext: When notice was given of the introduction of this bill to amend the Income War Tax Act, and of the one that follows, to amend the Salary Deduction Act, 1932, it was believed that by having them placed on the order paper, under the heading "Introduction of Bills," these bills could be proceeded with merely by introducing them in the ordinary course inasmuch as they were bills proposing to continue existing acts for a further period of a year. It subsequently transpired that there is a specific rule of the house which requires that a tax measure must be preceded by a resolution. Under these circumstances I would ask the unanimous consent of the house, to accept this notice of introduction as notice of the resolution, in which event I would move that the house do to-morrow resolve itself into committee of the whole to consider the proposed resolution. The advantage of that course would be that we could proceed to-morrow with the resolution; otherwise, the next government day being Friday, we should be precluded from the consideration of the resolution until Friday. In these circumstances I would ask whether I might have the unanimous consent of the house. If not, it only remains for me to put the notice on the order paper and wait until Friday.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT GOVERNMENT GIVE IMMEDIATE ATTENTION TO QUESTION OF DEBTS AND INTEREST RATES
PROPOSAL THAT GOVERNMENT GIVE IMMEDIATE ATTENTION TO QUESTION OF DEBTS AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Whereas; the question of public and private indebtedness has become one of our greatest and most perplexing problems, enhanced during the past years by the extremely low price level of all primary commodities, through which this indebtedness must be in large part met, and the effect of which has been to double and treble the actual burden of these liabilities; and,
Whereas; this fact has been recognized in respect of certain international obligations, and has become a practical issue in respect of the public obligations of many countries; and, Whereas; no such recognition has as yet been given to the heavy private indebtedness within this country, although these, together with the high interest rates which prevail, constitute 
just as heavy and impossible a burden to the individual, as do national and international obligations to the countries concerned; and,
Whereas; this situation is one of the greatest factors in the present economic depression, and is one of the greatest barriers to the financial recovery of agriculture and industry, and as such, deserves and commands the immediate attention of this parliament;
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, the government should give serious and immediate attention to the question of debts and interest rates within this country, and the possibility of their reduction, either by way of direct action, or by the submission of the entire problem to a special committee of this house, in order that the subject may be fully inquired into, and if possible, some solution found.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution which stands in my name and which is now before the house deals with a problem and presents a situation which is familiar to most hon. members and which, I think, demands the serious consideration of us all. In drafting this resolution and its preamble I have endeavoured to make it, so far as possible, selfexplanatory, so that it will contain within itself not only an indication as to the problem involved but one or two of the main arguments in support of the suggestion which is made, that suggestion being contained in the germane part of the resolution and asking that the government take into serious consideration the possibility of some reduction being made in the debts and interest of the people of this country, whether that reduction may be made by way of direct action or whether the subject may be dealt with through the appointment of a committee or in some other manner.
It might be said that I have not been very definite in this resolution. Not only do I admit the fact that I have made no definite suggestion as to the percentage of reduction which is necessary or which might take place, or as to the method which might be followed in applying such a reduction, if one were found possible, but I have purposely refrained from attempting to speak in a definite and dogmatic manner, for I recognize as clearly as does any other hon. member that this subject is one of tremendous difficulty; that it is fraught with complexities and that it can be approached only with great care and dealt with after careful consideration and deep thought.
Owing to the fact that my time is limited I shall not try to deal with the matter in other than a somewhat superficial way. Did my time permit, I should be glad to go into it in a more fundamental manner, and to discuss the question as to whether the growth

Economic Conditions-Mr. Speakman
of debt was an inevitable and integral part of the system under which we live and whether it were possible under any circumstances for the debts of the world to be paid. But as my time is limited I shall confine myself to the more obvious phases of the situation.
I have stated that I am aware of the difficulties that are involved. I am also aware of many of the criticisms which might and undoubtedly will be advanced in respect of such a suggestion, and with your permission, sir, I shall endeavour to anticipate one or two of the more serious and obvious. It might be suggested in the first place that this question of debt reduction, so far at least as it applied to agriculture, was at this time wholly academic in that now and under present conditions it makes little difference to the average farmer whether his debts stand as at present or whether they are materially reduced, as in few cases on the farm is the farmer able out of existing prices to pay any part of that indebtedness, as it now stands or if reduced. But I must point out in connection with that objection, first, that this resolution does not confine itself wholly to agricultural indebtedness but deals with indebtedness as a whole and, second, that we surely may anticipate that there will be some change in the situation. As a matter of fact, were we to follow that line of action or of inaction which led to an indefinite perpetuation of the present situation at least in respect of agriculture, we might accurately anticipate, not that the question of debt reduction would be one of prime urgency, but that not only would agriculture itself gradually become bankrupt but those who are directly or indirectly dependent upon agriculture would follow that pursuit into bankruptcy. Whether by the flux of time- and I doubt this-or by definite action taken, I am taking it for granted that some change in the situation must be brought about, and when that time comes, then the question of debt and its payment becomes one of immediate and urgent consideration.
It might also be suggested by way of criticism that in this resolution I am calling upon a federal government to consider matters which, under our constitution, are outside federal competence. I have no such purpose in mind nor am I suggesting that the federal or any other government should exceed the bounds of its own constitutional jurisdiction. I am not suggesting that we should ignore the law as it stands, but I am proposing that among the various govern-53719-115J
mental authorities, federal and provincial, within this country, in cooperation and joint action lie sufficient power and authority to deal not only with the question of debt, but with any other question in which the general good of the Canadian people is so deeply involved. I am suggesting that this government might well consider the question to the extent of its own jurisdiction and competence and, realizing that a part at least of the question of interest lies within federal competence, might take the lead, as the senior body, if one might so term it, within Canada in bringing about conference and cooperation as between itself and the provincial governments with the object of deciding upon and, if possible, putting into effect some policy which would relieve this intolerable burden. That is as far as my suggestion goes. I might further suggest along the same lines, that the federal government, as a federal government, is deeply concerned and that the resolution now before us might also contain a reference to the international situation and the part which Canada must play.
The other criticism which might well be advanced, and which as a matter of fact has been advanced throughout the country, is one touching the financial morality of such a suggestion. There is the question as to whether or not by any action, governmental or otherwise, bodies, individuals, corporations or countries which have loaned money should be deprived of a part of their rights when they demand repayment. There is the question as to whether we should suggest that a creditor organization which has loaned, say, $1,000 some years ago should now content itself with the receipt of $500. I use these figures arbitrarily and merely by way of illustration. In this connection ! would ask the question: What was loaned at that time? Money? Yes. But what is money? I am not going to enter into an academic discussion concerning money, but I am going to suggest that, after all, what was actually loaned had in itself no intrinsic value. What was loaned was potential purchasing power, potential goods, potential commodities, potential service. In other words what was loaned was the equivalent of certain goods or services which might be rendered. To my mind there is nothing unjust in the suggestion that in these days of public stress, in these times when eveiy citizen in the land is sharing or should share the effects of present conditions, we should at least consider the question as to whether it would not be perfectly fair to return to the creditor the same value in purchasing power, the same value in respect
1820	COMMONS
Economic Conditions-Mr. Speakman
of goods and services purchased, as had been advanced, together with fair interest. To my mind that is a matter which might well be considered; it is a question which few have answered, and it is a suggestion which will come within the strictest bounds of financial morality.
Then there is another aspect of the matter which is much more serious. We are well aware that during a war-in fact at any time of public emergency-the legal right of individuals must at times give way to the public weal. I am suggesting there is more involved in this matter of debt than merely a legal demand upon some person to repay a sum of money borrowed, than merely the legal right of some individual or corporation to receive repayment of a sum loaned. There is the question of the effect of the debt situation upon the entire community, upon the welfare of all the people and of the state itself. To my mind not only is there a tremendous question involved but in this situation there is a definite menace to the well being of all of us. After all, concerning certain classes of international indebtedness, it has been recognized throughout the world that the repayment of such debts, even if possible, would be detrimental to the public weal-would be detrimental alike to both the loaning and borrowing countries. That was recognized fully in respect of the German war reparations. Step by step, period after period, conference after conference, the demands for reparations have been reduced until at Lausanne those demands were practically wiped out. They were not, in my view, wiped out from any altruistic motives; they were wiped out because of the definite recognition on the part of the allies that they would suffer equally with the country called upon to make the payments. The allies recognized that the withdrawal annually of those large sums of money from the current purchasing power of the world, that the payment of those moneys without a corresponding exchange of goods, was detrimental to public interest and a definite handicap to the restoration of trade. The same argument could be applied with equal power and equal truth to other classes of war debts. It will be noted that to-day the statesmen of the world recognize that fact, and not only is debtor country after debtor country defaulting or threatening to default, repudiating or threatening to repudiate payment of the moneys they owe, but even Great Britain herself, whose financial morality has never been questioned, and who has prided herself upon her ability and willingness at 
all times to pay every dollar when due, has come to the conclusion, and has so notified her chief creditor, that some different arrangement must be made, and that the latest payment she made may be the last under present circumstances.
Again, Mr. Speaker, the withdrawal of that percentage of current purchasing power, the absorption of that portion of the national income along unproductive lines is a menace and barrier to future trade recovery. To my mind it is the impelling motive, and will be the impelling motive when these arrangements are perfected, and when these debts in large part will be-and I believe they will be-wiped out and cancelled. After all- and this is a somewhat paradoxical situation -the ill effects of payments of international debts is felt just as much by the creditor nation as the debtor nation. To-day we have the seeming anomaly of the United States, the chief creditor country of the world, declaring on the one hand a definite policy providing for debt repayment, and, on the other hand recognizing, as every country must recognize, that in the last resort those debts must be paid in goods, refusing to accept payment in that form. She realizes that such payment would not only inflict hardship upon the country charged with payment, but would inflict greater hardship upon herself. To avoid that eventuality they have raised barriers to prevent the payment of those debts in goods, because if the debt were paid in that way great quantities of goods would be admitted into the country without calling for the export of other commodities in return. Nations of the world are beginning to realize that such a situation would end in the closing of factories of the creditor country, and a tremendous increase in unemployment figures. I cannot but believe that what applies to war debts or reparations must apply with equal force to other forms of international indebtedness. Every factor which makes it impossible or inadvisable to pay war debts in full operates to exactly the same degree and in exactly the same way in respect of all other international obligations. There may be a difference of course, from an academic point of view, or from the point of view of financial morality, if you will-a difference in the origin of the debts, or a difference in the purpose for which those debts were incurred. But from the business point of view, and that is the aspect from which I choose to discuss it, there is no difference in the effects of the repayment, or the demand for repayment, as between one form of international liability and another.

Economic Conditions-Mr. Speakman
Now as my time is passing rapidly and, as these arguments are being given increasing recognition throughout the countries of the world, may I suggest that some of them apply with almost equal force to internal and private indebtedness? When we survey the debt situation throughout the world and endeavour to compute the amount which is now owing we find a sum which is so huge as to stagger the imagination. Four hundred billion dollars, the computed amount of world indebtedness, means nothing to me personally. I can no more comprehend it than I can comprehend the computations by which astronomers measure the distances between stars or the speeds at which certain stars may travel in their orbits. Four hundred billion dollars means as little to me in actual effect as the distance represented by a light year. Any consideration of that sum, any question of repayment in full or even in large part becomes not only meaningless but positively ludicrous. When you consider that the interest alone at five per cent amounts to $20,000,000,000 a year on world obligations, I think it becomes obvious that the business of this world, the production of this world, the ability of this world to pay must fall infinitely short of that vast sum.
Now we turn to private indebtedness, internal indebtedness, the discussion of which is the main purpose of this resolution, and which to a much greater degree than international indebtedness is in out hands, within our own competence, and is a much more immediate and urgent problem as far as we are concerned. I have been endeavouring to compute with as great accuracy as possible the aggregate of debt within this country. I have been unable to arrive at an accurate computation, but roughly speaking, drawing upon the last census returns I find that in interest bearing bonds publicly issued, that is federal, provincial and municipal, we owe $4,600,000,000 of which $3,220,000,000 is owing in Canada and $1,380,000,000 outside of Canada. Then I find also that other bonded debts, that is of railway and other corporations, amounts to nearly as great a sum. I say "nearly"; a billion dollars less, but what is a billion dollars in view of sums such as I have indicated? Their bonded indebtedness amounts to something like S3,500,000,000, of which $1,500,000,000 is due in Canada and nearly $2,000,000,0000 due outside of Canada.
Then I find that mortgages upon farms amount to approximately $700,000,000. There is a question in doubt in regard to that, I have been unable to obtain satisfactory information as to whether that includes all forms of sale agreements on farms, some say
it does, some say it does not, I have been unable to ascertain from any of our authorities whether in taking the census all census takers treated those questions alike, and secondly, as to what actually was involved. But the weight of opinion is that this does not include agreements of sale, but only mortgages, where the money has been actually loaned to an individual already owning his land. And this total does not include mortgages on town or city property, but only farm mortgages.
Then I find that the sums owiing to banks of this country by individuals and corporations amounts to somewhere about . $2,500,000,000. Again I have been unable to get definite details as to that indebtedness, but that figure is given me from the census office from the best authorities that I can consult as approximately the amount owing to the banks at the present time.
These figures then, totalling about $12,000,000,000, can be taken as fairly definite. But they do not include, as I say, mortgages on town or city property, it is unlikely that they include amounts owing on sales agreements on farm and other properties, and they do not include the vast total of relatively small debts owing by various individuals and companies, to retail stores for instance. So I think it would be safe to estimate that you can add another five or six billion, but I shall confine myself to the $12,000,000,000 definitely indicated, merely suggesting that this is not the whole. A tremendous load, you will say, upon a population the size of ours. Including interest it calls for an enormous percentage of our national income. As to the interest charges, that again is somewhat uncertain because the rate of interest varies greatly, from perhaps 4i per cent in some favoured cases, 5 per cent on some classes of bonds, up to 8, 9, and 10 per cent upon certain classes of mortgages and other liabilities. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I know that in many cases, through fees, charges on renewals, compounding of interest, it amounts to as high as 12 and 14 per cent for some unfortunate people. But even if you take it on an average at 6 per cent and apply it only to the $12,000,000,000 of which we have definite record we have a sum of $720,000,000 a year due in interest, an amount double or treble the entire value of this last year's wheat crop.
Now what is the effect of that? I must deal with it very briefly, and merely from two aspects. First as to the effect on the public weal, using the term commonly used, one expressing a situation of very great importance. What is the effect of the with-
1822	COMMONS
Economic Conditions-Mr. Speakman
drawal from channels of consumption, from current purchasing power, of so large a sum? Of even so large a sum as that part which is paid? It must be remembered in this connection that a large part of these annual payments is due, not to men of moderate means, who will spend the greater part of their income in the purchase of commodities or services, but to men or corporations whose income already covers their needs, and the bulk of whose surplus income must go not into purchasing channels but into investment. Now investment is necessary and good. But the common form of investment is either bonds or additions to our productive plant or its improvement. No matter how it is invested it is not added to the purchasing income of this nation in respect to its purchase of goods.
What is the effect of its withdrawal from current purchasing power? The effect is obvious on all sides, in every country. As you withdraw purchasing power-it is true that this is only one factor in the situation- the inevitable result must be unsold goods and crashing price levels. Both of those conditions are with us to-day, and to this the debt situation, the payment of debt and of interest as far as it is paid, is one of the main contributing factors. It is for the public good- including the cerditors in this country-to see a revival of trade, an increase in the price level of primary commodities, a general speeding up of the wheels of industry. This can only be accomplished through an acceleration of and adding to the means of consumption. I must leave that, for time will not permit any detailed discussion of the point.
Now I come to the effect of debt on the private individual-its damning and crushing effect-and if I confine myself largely to its effect on agriculture it is from no lack of realization that it applies with equal force and weight to other industries and individuals; but I am familiar with its effect on agriculture, and I prefer to speak of that which I know. Take the case of the average farmer to-day-and I am not speaking now of the farmer whose position has always been hopeless; I am not speaking of the inefficient farmer, but the average farmer who is recognized by those who know him as being as efficient and courageous an individual as will be found in this country. As a matter of fact, when you take into consideration the ordinary vicissitudes of farm life, the uncertainties through climatic conditions which must always be the farmer's lot, you will recognize that to be a farmer continuously, to stay with the job year in and year out throughout a lifetime, requires courage, 
patience, perseverence and optimism of no mean order. But he is content with that.
Consider, however, the' situation of these men to-day. Some years ago, for purposes of increased production, in some cases because of the encouragement offered by the high price levels, because of the demand made on the farmer for increased production, because of governmental and financial encouragement, many of these men, too many of them, went into debt. I am not discussing the question whether or not they Should have gone into debt. I suppose if our foresight had been as good as our hindsight, many of us would have acted differently four or five years ago than we did. But they did go into debt for business purposes, and certainly for purposes perfectly meritorious. They borrowed money, mortgaged their farms and other property as security for the payment of that money, and anticipated at that time, as they had every right to anticipate from the price levels, the general conditions, future prospects, and from the optimistic statements of every political and financial leader in the country, that they would be able to borrow in safety and repay when the time came.
Prices crashed and this money, we must remember, was borrowed at that time mainly on high prices. That statement will go unchallenged. Certainly no farmer has borrowed, at any rate very few farmers have borrowed any money since prices fell. No money has been loaned since that time. So that I am safe in saying that the debt was incurred on high price levels. Now the farmer finds himself with a debt which was a moderate and reasonable one at the time it was incurred, bearing not too great a proportion to the value of his assets; but to-day under any fair appraisal-and I am not speaking now of forced Sale when land and stock are worth practically nothing, but of fair appraisal- to-day, I say, under any fair appraisal, tens of thousands of these men owe more money than the entire value of their assets; and if the ordinary rules of bankruptcy were put into force, that is to say, the ability to pay when due the amount due, they would be bankrupt. Of course, they are not bankrupt now in that sense, because no one is attempting to foreclose, or very few. No mortgage company or bank, no individual wants to take a security which has become a liability; they do not want to find themselves obliged to pay taxes on the land. At the present time therefore the land is reasonably safe. But the farmers find themselves confronted with a debt greater in amount than the

Economic Conditions-Mr. Speakman
entire value of their property, and with an income reduced enormously through the crash of prices.
Let me give one slight illustration. There is a man whom I know very well who borrowed a relatively small sum-$2,000. He borrowed at a time when the price of wheat in my locality was a little over a dollar net to the farmer. He was unable to pay because the price fell shortly after the tame he borrowed. To-day wheat is worth, roughly, 25 cents a bushel at the country point in my district, for No. 1, as compared with a dollar and a few cents three years ago. That means that while he borrowed the value of 2,000 bushels of wheat he must pay 8,000 bushels in return. Now, wheat itself has not lost its value; it is as valuable for food purposes as ever it was. But it has lost its value in relation to other goods and principally in relation to money. This man is called upon to pay that increased number of bushels of wheat. It is not merely a matter of his debt having quadrupled; his ability to meet his indebtedness has been cut far more than four times. A man farming pays his debts out of the surplus left after he has paid his cost of living, operating expenses and taxes. Even were there a modicum left to-day, you will realize that it takes a far greater percentage of 25 cent per bushel wheat to maintain his farm and keep his family than when wheat was worth a dollar. The surplus left therefore, if any, is a much smaller proportion of the entire crop than at the time wheat was higher; and yet that smaller surplus is worth only one-quarter as much per bushel. So that the debt-paying ability of the farmer has been cut eight or ten times, even if the price has fallen only three-quarters.
Now what will this man do? You will say to him, carry on. Surely; he is carrying on in the hope and confident trust that times will improve, in the confidence that the mortgage company will not foreclose, for reasons I have indicated, or that the provincial government will step in with some protection and prevent foreclosure. But what then? The man is not paying that principal; he is not paying his interest. As a matter of fact he has cut his standard of living to the bone. In doing so he is leaving goods unpurchased on the shelves in the stores. This results in factory wheels being slowed down, thus adding to unemployment. He has cut his operating costs, and that means that he is reducing the efficiency of his farm for the future. He is allowing weeds to grow because he cannot keep them under control; he is allowing the place to fall into disrepair because he cannot keep it in proper
condition; his fences are falling in because he cannot repair them; his machinery is wearing out because he cannot replace it; and his efficiency is being reduced not through any fault of his own but because that is involved in the lower cost of operation. He is paying his taxes if he can. But he sees year by year not only that unpaid amount remaining but the accumulation of interest. His debt is increasing, and there is a situation which is breaking the hearts and threatening to break the morale of the most courageous and optimistic lot of men in the country.
I am asking to-day that in view of these circumstances the government should do something-not that they should step in and immediately cut debts; no. I am asking, however, that they take into serious consideration the possibility of this being done; that they acquire all the knowledge and the experience that men may give them; that they discuss it with those who are interested in cooperating and in endeavouring to remove part of the burden. For it is obvious to all that it is not only the individual who suffers; but the nation itself, under that load, when faced with the upward trend, which we hope is ahead of us, will be hampered and weighed down so that the climb into that prosperity which we are all hoping for will be retarded. May I repeat that I am asking for nothing unfair. It is the duty of every citizen of this country to bear his or her share of the troubles which lie upon the land. Amidst the crash of falling values when stocks have disappeared, when men onoe wealthy have become poor, when farms have become liabilities, when primary goods can be hardly given away and when retail goods have been left upon the shelves, one commodity, one set of men are standing untouched-money itself has retained and is increasing its actual value. It is a misnomer and a mistake to treat money as a commodity and to my mind it is a most ridiculous and anomalous situation that when the value of the real wealth of the land has fallen, the value of the symbol itself remains untouched or has actually increased in value. It is not right that one class of mien, the creditor class, should be immune in an emergency which is crushing and threatening the nation itself.
I am not asking for anything unreasonable and I have endeavoured to avoid speaking in a political, a critical or a partial manner. I am not imputing blame to any government, as no government in itself has been responsible. Certain governmental actions have added to the situation, but the difficulty lies in the system under which we live and move.
1824	COMMONS
Economic Conditions-Mr. Guthrie
I am speaking of this matter from the point of view of what I believe to be practical business and common humanity. I fervently hope that the house will consider this matter from the same point of view, that it will give its unbiased consideration, its most intelligent thought and considered vote in an effort to assist the people of this country and of the world in removing a burden which can no longer be borne.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT GOVERNMENT GIVE IMMEDIATE ATTENTION TO QUESTION OF DEBTS AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we will all agree that the hon. member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Speakman) lias brought to the attention of this house a serious problem which confronts not only the people of this country but of all civilized countries of the world, namely, the question of debt and the question of interest. In reading the motion which the hon. member moved I notice that apparently he intended to confine its scope to what one might call the domestic debts of the Dominion of Canada; in his motion he asks that the immediate attention of this house should be given to the question of debts and interest rates within this country. While in his opening remarks he elaborated quite fully his own views with regard to what one might call the international financial situation throughout the world, I think he intends his motion to apply more particularly to what I might describe as the domestic situation or the question of national, provincial, municipal and private debts within the borders of the Dominion of Canada.
The figures which he gave to the house with regard to these various classes of debts I think produced something in the nature of a shock. Personally, I had no idea that the aggregate indebtedness at this moment of the Dominion of Canada was anything approaching the figure of twelve billions of dollars; I thought the total amount would have been much less. These figures stated by the hon. member are so enormous that I think the house should take serious note of the situation as it exists to-day. When one contemplates the aggregate debt of the country one must also contemplate the aggregate amount of interest which is payable annually in respect of such debt. As I understand this motion its purpose is to induce this house or a committee of this house to give serious and careful study to this important and pressing problem. As the hon. member elaborated his ideas I thought that he was perhaps a little academic and a little theoretical in his treatment of the situation and I was inclined to think that he should have offered something 
in the nature of a practical suggestion as to what might be achieved to the end asked for in his motion.
In this country there are roughly four chief divisions of indebtedness. First, there is the public debt, in which term we include national debts, provincial debts and municipal debts. Then, there is another type of debt which is also a public debt namely, our railway debts. I always include railway debts when considering the public debt of this country. There is yet another vast amount of indebtedness which has to be considered namely, that of the great corporations of this country. Private corporations have raised large amounts of money by bonds and otherwise both in this and other countries, and these obligations must be considered to some extent at least as public debts of the country. Unfortunately, a large proportion of these corporation debts are held and are payable outside of Canada and this fact rather adds to the burden which we have to bear in respect to them both in connection with the payment of principal and the payment of annual interest.
We then come to what we might call the private debts of the country, the debts which the people of the country owe to each other, to the banks, to the loan companies, and to individuals. In respect of all these debts interest is payable. Under the act which constituted the Dominion of Canada the matter of interest was placed among those subjects which come within the exclusive jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. By subsection 19 of section 91 of the British North America Act, interest is specifically mentioned as being one of the subjects to be dealt with exclusively by this parliament. To many it may come as news that there is in existence an act of this parliament known as the Interest Act. Unfortunately or fortunately in dealing with the subject of interest this parliament has to a very large extent divested itself of authority in respect of past transactions. The second section of this act provides:
Except as otherwise provided by this or by any other act of the parliament of Canada, any person may stipulate for, allow and exact, on any contract or agreement whatsoever, any rate of interest or discount which is agreed upon.
Parliament in its wisdom has left the question of interest almost entirely at the will of the people who enter into contracts or make bargains. The only practical enactment contained in the Interest Act having application to past transactions, is to be found in the third section which provides that where no interest is stipulated in the bargain or agree-

Economic Conditions-Mr. Guthrie
ment, five per cent shall be the maximum amount which may be chargeable.
It is true that there are provisions in the act with regard to the rate of interest which may be charged upon mortgages, but these provisions are not what one would describe as being provisions of practical utility. For instance, in respect of mortgages it is merely provided that where the payment of principal and interest is combined as in the instalment plan that a specific rate of interest must be stated in the mortgage and no greater rate can be charged. There is also provision that where a mortgage extends beyond a period of five years it can always be paid off at the end of the five year period by tendering the amount of the mortgage plus three months' interest in advance by way of bonus. The same section also provides that after such a tender no further interest may be charged. These are practically the only items of general utility mentioned in the Interest Act.
We have a number of special acts which deal with interest. We have in the Bank Act provisions in regard to the rate of interest. We have in the Exchequer Court Act provisions under which five per cent only can be charged. We have in the Expropriation Act and in the Bills of Exchange Act provisions in relation to interest. We have likewise on our statute books an act known as the Moneylenders' Act under which I think the maximum amount chargeable by way of interest is 12 per cent, but that act applies only to loans under $500, so that the Moneylenders' Act is one of very limited application. One may state in general that this country, whatever rate of interest may be agreed upon between the borrower and the lender, such rate will have to be paid, except under certain specific acts some of which I have just mentioned. So far this parliament has not taken any very definite action in regard to the question of interest although its jurisdiction in respect of that subject is certainly exclusive and, I believe, unquestioned. To a large extent parliament has left the question of interest to be agreed upon by the borrower and the lender.
The practical question is:	How are we
going to proceed to reduce the debt and interest in Canada and at the same time be just, do no wrong to any party concerned? It will be readily understood that most of our contracts and agreements, in fact one might almost say all of them, are made under the authority of provincial laws; they all touch the great question of property and civil rights; they are contracts upon which this parliament of Canada has no right to legislate.
The only legislative right of this parliament would be to fix the rate of interest; but this parliament has already expressly provided in the Interest Act that the parties themselves may stipulate and agree in regard to the rate of interest which shall be charged. After having given parties the right to negotiate, to make their own agreements in respect of interest, would it be wise or proper for this parliament now to intervene and in any way to alter or vary rights arising under contracts and agreements which we have permitted to be made and where various interest rates have been agreed to between the parties?
There may be some means, which does not for the moment present itself to me, of meeting a situation of this kind. No practical suggestion was offered in regard to the matter by my hon. friend who moved the motion. If there is a prospect of reaching a solution of the problem, of finding a remedy for the pressing situation which undoubtedly exists in this country as regards both debt and interest, the house will certainly welcome the opportunity. I notice my hon. friend in his motion asks that a committee of this house should study the question and report upon it. I would heartily agree with his suggestion. Perhaps a special committee might be best for the purpose, but in my judgment I think a question of this kind might well be studied by the banking and commerce committee. That, however, is not a matter of importance. The banking and commerce committee is already constituted and I think at present embraces in its numbers all or practically all hon. members who are most familiar with the subject of finance, public debt, banking, interest and the like My suggestion-and it is only a suggestion -would be that this particular question should be referred to that committee to be dealt with at the present session, and if any solution can be found which will assist us in reducing rates of interest or in reducing the public and private debts of this country, then my hon. friend will be entitled to congratulations in regard to debt from every corner of the dominion.
I am not dealing at all with the international situation; I am at the moment referring only to those debts which are hampering us in this country and those burdensome interest payments which we are called upon annually to make in Canada. Whether from private individuals, corporations, municipalities, provinces, or from the Dominion treasury, I cannot recognize much distinction between them. They are all oppressive; they
1826	COMMONS
Economic Conditions-Mr. Guthrie
are all burdensome. I think I can admit that I did not fully realize the enormous amount of indebtedness of this country until I listened to the figures submitted to the house this afternoon by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman). I suppose an ideal state for this or any other country would be to have no debts, either public or private. Indeed we may well recall the words of William Shakespeare when he says:
Neither a borrower nor a lender be,
For loan oft loses both itself and friend;
And borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry.
However we may never reach thait happy condition. Business has to be carried on in this, and every other country by means of credit. The question is: What rate of interest must we pay for the credit which is necessary for the conduct of business? Is there any practical way of controlling interest rates except through the inexorable law of supply and demand? Personally, I trust this motion may pass this house and that the whole question may be referred either to a special committee or to the committee on banking and commerce, and let me express the hope that the committee, to whichever one it is referred, may bring in something in the nature of practical conclusions from which we may eventually obtain some relief.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT GOVERNMENT GIVE IMMEDIATE ATTENTION TO QUESTION OF DEBTS AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad indeed to second the resolution moved by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) and I am sure hon. members will join with me in congratulating him on the clarity and forcefulness with which he presented the subject matter of this resolution to the house. I should also like to congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) on the manner in which he has accepted the resolution and advised the house to pass it and refer it to a committee. He stated that the hon. member for Red Deer had not offered any practical solution to this question. We are all looking for solutions, and the idea of the hon. member was that instead of a solution being offered by him, the question should go before a committee of the house where it would receive the benefit of the combined wisdom of the members of that committee in offering a practical solution to deal with this all-important question, one which I 'think touches the very lives of the people at the present time.
When one speaks of scaling down debts, this is looked upon by some as repudiation and therefore with disfavour, but in my opinion the average individual is honest and wishes, if at all possible, to liquidate his

undertakings, I believe hon. members will agree that we are facing at present entirely new world conditions. As the Right Hon. Winston Churchill, speaking on the last British budget, says:
As I left the politics of yesterday for those of to-da.v, I now leave the polities of to-day for those of to-morrow.
In other words, what was good for yesterday may not be good for to-day or to-morrow, so we have to change our outlook according to the general conditions with which we are confronted. When we come to the question of debts I am sure most hon. members, including the Minister of Justice, have certainly been shocked by the startling figures presented to the house this afternoon by the hon. member for Red Deer. I am not going to repeat those figures, because they are already on Hansard.
Coming down to the question of farm debts, I shall direct my remarks more particularly to conditions obtaining in the province of Alberta, from which I come. It is not my wish to cast any reflection upon those engaged in taking census information, but I suggest there is at least a doubt as to whether or not the figures as shown in the census reports present a true picture. I find from those reports that there are 97,408 farms in the province of Alberta. Of that number 34,305 reported debts, Showing a total debt of 8108,463,700. In other words only 35 per cent of Alberta farms report encumbrance, and the natural conclusion would be (that 65 per cent are clear of debt. I believe any hon. member who is familiar with conditions in western Canada will agree it is hard to believe that 65 per cent of western farms are in that fortunate position. We know, further, that apart from mortgages there are many other debts. Before a committee of the Alberta legislature sitting about a year ago the fact was brought out that the retail merchants in that province alone had on their books debts totalling over $40,000,000. We know that those debts in most cases were contracted in good faith, but that the price levels at which they were contracted were much higher than they are to-day. As everyone knows the price of farm products to-day has dropped approximately 60 per cent, while the cost of living has dropped only about 20 per cent. Farm prices have been cut more than 50 per cent while debts, mortgages, interest rates and other charges have remained the same. It is generally recognized to-day by all well informed people that war debts must be cancelled. In this connection I should

Economic Conditions-Mr. Lucas
like to quote the words of Mr. Chamberlain, as they appear in the press of recent date:
Now in pointing out what would be the effect of resuming war debt payments, I am not using threats. If you see a man walking along a precipice and you point out to him that the ground just in front of him is^ undermined, that is not a threat, it is a warning, and it is not less friendly because it is evident that if the man goes over the precipice he is quite likely to drag you down with him.
I believe that is a point we should all keep in view, because it is becoming generally recognized that to force payment at the present time is just about as harmful to the creditor as the debtor. While there is a general feeling that war debts must be cancelled I think we must come to the conclusion that the same process must be applied to governmental and private debts. I have before me a copy of the Toronto Saturday Night of February 4, a publication printed in Toronto, the financial centre of Ontario. In it I find the following:
That it is time something was done to readjust the relations between debtor and creditor, so far as the sovereign power of Canada can properly readjust them, becomes daily more evident. We do not think the east of Canada fully appreciates the tremendous force behind the demand for readjustment of interest rates- even on old contracts-in the west.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT GOVERNMENT GIVE IMMEDIATE ATTENTION TO QUESTION OF DEBTS AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
This resolution, Mr. Speaker, deals with a subject which is very prominently before the people of Canada at the present time. People everywhere are discussing it; indeed one of the most hopeful signs on the horizon at the moment is that interest in economic problems such as this is widespread and general. Clearly the primary producers are being discouraged and crushed by the burden of debt and interest charges, and everyone recognizes the necessity of some adjustment between the debtor and creditor classes. If there is one point I would like to make clear and emphasize, it is the fact that recovery in general is inseparably bound up with the recovery of agriculture in particular. Everywhere we find stagnation in business. This is due largely to lack of purchasing power, the sources of which in Canada are largely the sale of products of the forest, the mine, the sea and the land. Of these primary products agriculture is the most important, because some forty-seven per cent of the people of Canada are engaged in agriculture. When our agriculturists are in the red, as it were, there can be no prosperity, because the curve indicating the progress and welfare of the agriculturists is reflected in the curve marking the prosperity of Canada in general. Mr. Wilson, of the Royal Bank, made the statement recently that during the past year interest rates on bonds had fallen from 5.20 to 4.83 per cent. This is a small reduction; it is nothing compared with that which has taken place in the prices of primary products. Certainly the value of money has remained up, whereas the value of other things has greatly depreciated.
I desire at this time to put on Hansard a few figures from the Minneapolis Tribune, showing that the production of wheat has more than doubled during the last forty years. In the United States of America it has increased from 378,000,000 bushels to
890,000,000 bushels; in Canada from 42,000,000 to nearly 400,000,000 bushels; in the Argentine from 31,000,000 to 219,000,000 bushels; in Australia from 27,000,000 to 171,000,000 bushels; in India from 229,000,000 to 347,000,000 bushels. In Canada we have a crop usually somewhere around 400,000,000 bushels. We can only use 100,000,000 for food and seed, so we are faced with the necessity of marketing between 200,000,000 and 300,000,000 
bushels. I believe that the difficulty in distributing this amount would have been much less had we some sixteen or eighteen months ago followed Great Britain and some twenty-one other countries in going off the gold standard. Where can we find a market? The countries of Europe,-France, Italy, Germany,-have high tariff barriers against our wheat. Great Britain cannot take it all. For years we looked with hope to the Orient. We saw there a great potential market, with hundreds of millions of hungry people, but recently we have lost that market. According to the figures from Mr. Marler's office, referred to the other night, we have lost it to Australia, because in 1928 we supplied 51 per cent of the wheat imported by Japan, and at present we are supplying only 13 per cent, just enough for blending purposes. Australia in 1928 supplied only 12 per cent, and to-day is supplying 84 per cent. So that great market is gone. Also the flour millers of this country have in the past supplied the Orient with large quantities of low grade flour. Recently some of them tendered for contracts; if they had received those contracts their mills would have been occupied for a long time. Unfortunately for us the contract went to Australia, because Australia was able to make more use of the money of China. The premier of Australia pointed out recently that his country by the action it had taken had been able to improve very much its desperate financial condition. Why is Australia taking from us the market that we so badly need? Why is it possible for them to get flour contracts, sell their crop and improve their financial condition? I think the answer is clear; they have depreciated their currency, when world-wide deflation was sweeping over all countries. Canada, almost alone among the smaller nations of the world, has taken the full impact of deflation unchecked and unsoftened by any form of reflation. We have seen values crumbling around us, and no hand has effectively stopped them. Even to-day we are trying to pay debts that in present values, of wheat for example, amount to three or even four times what they amounted to when incurred. We find it very difficult to carry on trade; while people in New Zealand and Australia and the Argentine, who are our competitors, can sell their products in Great Britain and taking home the pound sterling find it worth S6 to $7, we in Canada in selling to Great Britain find the pound sterling in our country worth something like S3.80. How can we compete on an unfair basis such as that? Surely there has been much misery and suffering owing to the unfair position in which our producers find themselves.

Economic Conditions-Mr. Gershaw
In discussing some of the effects which deflation has had, I wish to put on Hansard a few figures taken from Stuart Chase's book entitled "The New Deal." I quote these figures because of their accuracy, although similar conditions could be found anywhere in our own country. A certain committee visited 6,304 families in New York. These families were unknown to the relief organization. They did not apply for relief. We find that 81 per cent lacked food; 88 per cent were in arrears for rent; 38 per cent lacked winter clothing; 25 per cent were short of fuel; 67 pea' cent were in arrears for life insurance; 74 per cent borrowed from relatives, and 1,500 families had pawned their furniture to buy food. That, remarks the author of this book, is what deflation means in human terms; that is the grim savagery of the business cycle downward. We need only look around us in Canada to see what deflation has meant here. We find that a debt which could have been paid in 1929 with 100 bushels of wheat now requires 400 bushels. Unemployment is mere widespread; financial stringency is greater; tariffs are higher and confidence is less. According to the definition, deflation is caused when the available supply of goods outruns the available supply of money, and it is quite easy for us to see how, in days like these, when new machinery is being invented and when more and more capital has been put into larger and larger factories-when these conditions exist, it is easy to see how the supply of goods could exceed the supply of money, and when that happens deflation occurs. It has happened before. History records that away back in the early ages the Roman Empire had a standard of living which until thait time had not been thought of. So long as they were able to get gold from the mines of Spain and Greece their prosperity continued, their standard of living was maintained. But when these mines were worked out and there was a shortage of gold, the Roman Empire declined and fell. Their rich fields were turned into pastures. Taxes were unpaid and Rome fell into an abyss and carried a large part of civilization with it.
Surely if this process of deflation continues we must take warning lest a similar fate befall our country at the present time. Repeatedly during the last century we have been threatened with disaster from deflation; many cycles of depression have come, and usually they have gone when some fresh supply of gold has been discovered. The discovery of gold in South Africa or in California or in the Klondyke has usually arrested
the downward trend and introduced a better standard of living, better prices and greater prosperity. That is what has happened time and again, whereas a shrinking of currency has resulted in lower prices and a lower standard of living.
Some figures were put on Hansard the other night by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) showing that at the present time we have a great shrinkage in currency. Dominion notes in the last twelve years have shrunk from 8320,000,000 to $161,000,000, and bank notes from $200,000,000 to $150,000,000, while bank loans have shrunk by $600,000,000. Deflation has resulted in a decrease in profits and an increase in fixed charges, and this has induced, first, caution and then fear and then the panic which we see at the present time.
In 1869, Senator Sherman of the United States, speaking on the effect of a contracting currency, said this:
To every person except the capitalist out of debt and the salaried person-
I assume he means the person whose salary has not been cut.
-it is a period of loss, lassitude of trade, the fall of wages, suspension of enterprise, bankruptcy and disaster.
Another book I have read recently points ouit that there are certain classes who suffer and suffer severely by deflation, and there is one class that suffers much less than others through this process. Deflation affects the active business man. If he is renting buildings his rent stays at about the same rate, whereas he finds that he has fewer sales, less cash and less in the way of profits. Deflation affects more particularly the primary producer, the producer of an exportable product, because of the lower prices which he receives for ithat product, and owing to the fact that interest and mortgages are stationary, his burden is relatively increased. Deflation is hard for labour because there is so much unemployment, and particularly hard for governments because budgets are unbalanced and the people are dissatisfied and discontented. Only the capitalist with vested interests may be fortunate enough to gain, if he has money invested and can secure the same rate of interest for it.
Other countries have faced difficulties such as confront us at the present time and have made attempts to stay the process of deflation. I find that as far back as 1790 inflation took place in France. At that time some 400,000,000 units of currency were issued, based on confiscated church property. There were some gainsayers even at that time, but
1830	COMMONS
Economic Conditions-Mr. Euler
othere could hardly contain themselves for joy when they anticipated the advantages of this action. The result of this particular effort was apparently quite successful. The treasury was relieved, a portion of the debt was paid, credit revived, trade increased and troubles seemed to vanish. It is quite possible that if the national authorities had stopped at that point no disaster would have ensued. No doubt they brought great relief to many of their citizens at that time. We read, of course, that later on they got into difficulties. The government was unwise enough to yield to temptation and followed the seductive path of unrestricted inflation.
Those who are so much afraid of inflation at the present time have in mind unrestricted inflation, whereas those who advocate some measure of inflation contemplate a controlled effort, not as a panacea for all our evils, but as something more desirable than drifting with the downward course of deflation without any effort at control. We are the custodians of all that has been gained and earned in the past, and surely with the experience before us of other nations and ages we should be able to act and still avoid the pitfalls which face those who carry on to fatal extremes. We know what the process of deflation has done to others, and we must guard our country and see that all that is modern in our civilization does not pass away. New Zealand, South Africa and other countries are keeping their currencies upon a suitable depreciated basis; why not Canada?

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT GOVERNMENT GIVE IMMEDIATE ATTENTION TO QUESTION OF DEBTS AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) has made so convincing an argument that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) on behalf of the government has consented to the appointment of a committee as requested in the resolution, it is probably a little out of place to attempt to discuss the merits or demerits of the question of debts and interest, and I may say to you, sir, that I do not intend to do so. The mere citation of the total amount of debts as being twelve billions of dollars, and the fact that governments, federal, provincial and municipal are obliged to pay some $700,000,000, annually in interest, presents an immediate argument for the consideration of this question, especially in view of the fact that it would seem to be impossible to continue to pay this interest. My principal reason in rising at this moment is not only to give my support to the resolution-this is not necessary since it is going to carry- but to deal for just a moment with another phase of the matter which has not been 
touched upon by my hon. friends from the west.
Quite naturally they have spoken of the difficulties of the western farmer-perhaps eastern farmers should be mentioned as well -but I have in mind a situation which is just as serious as that facing the farmer. If you look over the industrial towns and cities of the province of Ontario, cities like Windsor or Kitchener, you will find there literally thousands of men out of work. Two or three years ago these men owned their homes. They placed mortgages upon them, and they now find it not only impossible to pay the interest, but, like the farmer in the west, they are seeing the equities in their little homes absolutely wiped out. They are being left with nothing. Their difficulty is just as great as that being faced by any other class in the country. It seems to me that the trend must be in the direction of lower interest rates, especially so long as prices of commodities remain as they are at present.
It seems a solution which is offered apart from the preventing of future issues from bearing such high rates of interest, is what might be called repudiation. This is an action which none of us like to contemplate; countries pride themselves in carrying out their indebtedness, as do people, municipalities and provinces, but sometimes the necessity or, as the hon. member for Red Deer has said, the weal of the public generally requires remedies which otherwise would not be considered. I think it was about two years ago I made a suggestion to this house which, if hon. members paid any attention to it, rather shocked the house; I said that it might ultimately become necessary to have what might be called a capital levy. I also made another sugegstion along the lines of what may be considered by the committee to be appointed, I referred to the fact that the Jewish people in ages gone by had what they called a jubilee year every fifty years when all debts were wiped out. I commend that suggestion to the consideration of the committee. The suggestion is of course not really serious.
As has been stated, Australia has by process of legislation reduced the interest on her debts by something like twenty-two and one-half per cent. Great Britain has reduced the interest on some ten billions of dollars of securities from five per cent to three and a half per cent. I am inclined to think that the acceptance of the new bonds at the new rate of interest was not quite so voluntary as some of us might think.
I have really nothing more to say except that I do not quite agree with the Minister

Economic Conditions-Mr. Rhodes
of Justice when he stated that the hon. member for Red Deer had made no practical suggestions as to what might be done. I do not blame him for that; he has opened up the question and apparently he believes that in a multitude of counsellors there may be wisdom. I think he is quite right in leaving concrete proposals to the committee itself. I believe that the deliberations of this committee will serve the further purpose of bringing out information which will show the Canadian people the serious situation in which we are placed.

speechtext: How is that to be brought about?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT GOVERNMENT GIVE IMMEDIATE ATTENTION TO QUESTION OF DEBTS AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
How it is to be brought about is another matter entirely. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), having in mind the constitutional aspect, indicated that there were some very real difficulties in the way of practical solution of this subject. The hon. member for Red Deer recognized that fact. I do not wish to stress the constitutional difficulties in the way; I merely indicate that fact as an added circumstance, showing that

we have an additional difficult problem on our hands in dealing with the matter as compared with Australia, because in the latter country a few years ago the whole of the states' debts were taken over by the commonwealth and to-day there can be no increase in debt there except that- authorized by a public body which has been set up under statute. To put ourselves in a position comparable to that of Australia we would have to take over all the debts of the provinces and they would thus thereafter lose their autonomy in the matter of raising additional sums by borrowing.
My hon. friend said quite properly: Nevertheless the dominion is in a position to give a lead. Let me assure the hon. member and the house that the government is sensible of the difficulty and the importance of this subject and has given iit great consideration. Discussions have been had for a considerable period of time with responsible bodies throughout the country, including provinces, looking to some arrangement which would give a lead to the people at large in the matter of a reduction in interest charges. Further than that I would not at this stage wish to go lest my remarks might be given a wrong interpretation. I need only point out the fact that the government long since has recognized the desirability of reducing interest charges. As a matter of fact the conversion loan of two years ago was a step in that direction, and the magnitude of that operation at that time is not generally recognized in this country. There was converted then no less a sum than $638,600,000, or 60 per cent of the total bonds available for conversion, representing a conversion covering, in round figures, at least 25 per cent of our whole direct national obligation. The net result will be, when the full interest reduction comes into force in 1935-6, we shall have saved in interest annually no less a sum than $6,192,964.

speechtext:
The conversion loan interest, as the house is well aware, was four and a half per cent as against rates of interest of five and five and a half per cent on the bonds. It is one thing to pass a pious resolution as to the desirability of reducing interest charges; it is quite another to bring about that reduction, especially bearing in mind that the man who owns the money is the arbiter as to the interest he will receive if he chooses to lend, because so far even in utopian society I do not know of any method whereby an individual can be compelled to lend money.

Economic Conditions-Mr. Rhodes
Only last year we tried an experiment in a mild way in Canada. We brought out a national loan and bearing in mind the insistent demand that had been made, not only by public bodies but in parliament and in the press that we should have lower interest rates, we properly took heed of those voices. We tried mildy to give the people of Canada an opportunity to respond to that call. As a matter of fact, for the first time in Canada we issued bonds bearing a four per cent coupon. It is true it was offered to the public at the rate of 93.45, and at a price which yielded four and one-half per cent. That issue was made to the public on October 31, 1932. I have in my hand information showing the yield to the investor in dominion securities, as they were sold in the open market on November 1 of last year. The highest yield to be found in the list before me on comparable issues is on the 1943 issue and that issue yielded to the investor on that day 4.68. The lowest yield on any dominion issue in that range on that day was 4.57. Yet, would you believe it, that -07 per cent was sufficient to cause many individuals to refrain from purchasing our bonds yielding 4i per cent when they could go to the open market and buy one yielding 4.57. That trend is shown in a most eloquent way by an analysis of the figures showing purchases of that issue of last year. The total number of those who purchased bonds in S500 denominations was 3,784. Their purchases totalled
82,693,000,	or only 4.81 per cent of the total issue. Almost half of that issue or, to be exact, 47.32 per cent was purchased by large institutions. Those figures would show that the issue did not meet with popular response. It may be that the government should have made a greater effort by way of publicity although I must say that at the time we inaugurated that campaign we were criticized because we called to our assistance, by means of radio hookup, the premiers of the various provinces. It would seem therefore that we get criticism both ways.

It was the opinion of those identified with bond circulation that it was desirable to keep the 53719-116
cost of flotation and servicing to the lowest possible point. I may say that the cost of servicing coupons on smaller issues is out of all proportion to the amount of money received. It is true that after weighing the arguments one might conclude that it would be highly desirable to have distribution as wide as possible. It may be that we erred in not having smaller denominations in the last issue. In connection with a future issue, which will be larger, I have no doubt there will be an opportunity for the purchasers of small amounts to subscribe. I do not know that there is anything further I should say at this time. Any assistance we can render will be gladly given. We will cooperate in every possible way, and while I believe that the committee will face a very heavy task, and while I am fearful as to the results of its practical conclusions, I do know that it will embark upon its work with our blessing. May I go just a little farther than my colleague the Minister of Justice. As to the question whether the matter should be referred to the banking and commerce committee instead of to a special committee, I suggest my hon. friend would do well to amend his resolution so as to refer this subject specifically to the banking and commerce committee, a body set up deliberately for the purpose of settling matters of this kind. I believe that committee would give the subject as good if indeed not better consideration as a special committee, unless that special committee were composed of members of the banking and commerce committee. In that event there would be no object in not using the standing committee.

Would that be tying our
dollar to the pound?

speechtext:
No; it would be placing our dollar at its proper level, much nearer the proper level in gold countries than it is today. I think there is a great deal of misconception about the value of our dollar, about its being down so much; it is really the value of gold which has jumped around in the last three years, more than the value of sterling and the Canadian dollar. Canada, in her desperate attempt to keep up with gold, has deflated her currency much more than Australia, New Zealand and other countries that we are attempting to compete with. The result is that price levels are much lower in Canada than in nearly all those countries, and therefore the problem of debt is much more acute.
I support this resolution because so far I have been unable to interest the government in the question of raising the Canadian price level. Two years ago I said in this house that Canada should abandon the gold standard and allow her dollar to depreciate in foreign countries so as to raise commodity price levels in Canada. Had that been done, farmers and other producers in Canada, as well as working people, would not have been so terribly indebted to-day but would have been able to keep up their interest. There is no doubt in my mind that the bulk of our farmers could under such circumstances have kept up their interest payments. However, the government did not see fit to give much consideration to my proposal, so that deflation has continued while commodity prices have fallen steadily and debts and interest have continued to pile up. It was pointed out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), in the splendid speech which he made last year, that interest rates of eight, nine and ten per cent could not be paid at present price levels. The prices of agricultural products are so low that the farmers have no ability to pay interest at any rate
1836	COMMONS
Economic Conditions-Mr. Speakman
to-day. There are therefore only two alternatives: either find a way of doing what is suggested in this resolution, or we must raise commodity price levels. I would say that at the present time we must do both, because debts have continued to pile up on us until they have reached that point where in many cases we cannot take care of past indebtedness.
As suggested by the Minister of Finance, I am going to move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy), that the resolution be amended by striking out the words "a special committee of this house" and substituting therefor the words "the select standing committee on banking and commerce." If that is accepted by the house, I am sure it will be acceptable to the hon. member for Red Deer and a great many others of us, and I hope that when it is taken up it will receive very serious consideration and that we shall get from the committee some definite recommendation which will lead to a solution of this problem, one of the most important and most pressing in Canada to-day.
Amendment agreed to.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT GOVERNMENT GIVE IMMEDIATE ATTENTION TO QUESTION OF DEBTS AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
I have no intention of prolonging the debate, but I do wish to express my appreciation of the reception which this resolution has met throughout the house and particularly, may I say, on the part of the government as voiced by the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Finance. I have succeeded up to the limit of my most optimistic expectations for the time being.
I am perfectly prepared to accept the amendment, and that the matter be referred to the committee on banking and commerce, my sole purpose being to have the subject brought before a representative body of the house for the most careful investigation and study and in the hope that some results may accrue. I think there is no question that throughout the country a certain measure of relief and appreciation will be felt on the part of debtors, who form such an overwhelming majority of the population, at this evidence that their plight and this problem have been recognized by the house and the government, and that the house is at least taking the first necessary step towards studying and, if possible, meeting the situation.
It is unnecessary for mie to say more, save to reply to one or two suggestions or inferences on the part of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). The Minister of Justice was not exactly critical, although he seemied rather

disappointed; that I did not make, nor did I propose to make, any definite suggestion either as to the extent of the reduction which might be undertaken or as to the method which might be followed. I purposely refrained from this for the reason suggested by the Minister of Finance himself, that I felt it would be arrogating to myself more knowledge than I possess were I to assume that I had solved the problem in my own mind and that therefore it was unnecessary for other people to give any consideration to the problem. I think it is infinitely better for the committee itself, with all the means at its disposal, and all the evidence that will be adduced, to arrive at a solution. It would be far better to have a solution which was sound and businesslike, a practical solution, than one which would be more or less theoretical.
I also refrained from discussing any other aspects of the situation. The Minister of Finance rightly suggested that perhaps a better method would be to raise price levels. I agree, but the minister will recognize that they are two separate questions, although dealing somewhat with the same problem and having the same result in mind. From my experience I have found that the less involved you make a proposition the better its chances are for possible success in the house. If you segregate it from all other suggestions you are likely to find that support which would be lacking if you linked up the question with some other point of view which might not be so acceptable. While, therefore, I should have been glad to discuss inflation, depreciation and all the various aspects of the problem, I felt it was wise to refrain from such discussion at this time.
I can only again express my appreciation of the support given and interest taken throughout the house, and my most sincere hope that the labour of the committee will not be wasted but that it will get to work promptly, taking its duties seriously, and that something worth while for the country will result.
Resolution as amended agreed to.

When endorsed by the members of this house, the resolution will result forthwith in a preliminary satisfactory solution of an heraldic problem -which is becoming more important nationally and imperially every day. Australia had her flag. New Zealand had hers, as also had South Africa; every self-governing dominion of the commonwealth of British nations, with the exception of Canada, had a distinctive flag-a flag
symbolic of its natiomi life. The comments of prominent Canadians as well as the lively discussion in the weekly and daily press of the country at the time showed the great interest there was in the question of a national emblem, in the maimer in which Canada had been placed in a ridiculous "equality of status" position during an imperial conference held in the capital city of our dominion. Everywhere there was a sentiment remedial action should be taken.
Further, may I say that during last October and November no private members' resolutions or bills came before the house, which explains -why this resolution is now before us. Because of the anything but normal conditions now prevailing throughout Canada, because of the unemployment rampant throughout the land, because of the interest charges which are bearing so heavily on our people, because of the avalanche of debts which are facing Canadians from ocean to ocean, because of the economic and industrial problems which face this country, because much time must be taken up in the consideration of all these matters, I am going to ask that the house postpone its consideration of this resolution.
. The fact that many Canadians are without food, clothing and shelter causes me to withhold this resolution until some future occasion when it may be discussed under more auspicious conditions, thus helping rather than perhaps hurting a cause so near and dear to all Canadians strong in their national and empire zeal and faith. When this time rolls around I hope parliament will come to a flag conclusion that will redound to the welfare of this country.
