subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT OFFICIAL NAME BE CHANGED FROM "DOMINION OF CANADA" TO "KINGDOM OF CANADA"

speechtext:
Mr. ARMAND R. LaVERGNE (Mont-magny) moved:
That in view of the statute of Westminster, the traditions of the Canadian people, and the constitution of the country, this house is of the opinion that the name of Canada should be changed from that of "The Dominion of Canada" to that of "Kingdom of Canada."
He said: Mr. Speaker, the resolution which stands in my name has been on the order

paper for the last two years and I feel I must apologize to the house for bringing it up only to-night. The first year I was prevented by the rules of procedure and also by some more pressing business, from bringing it up. Last year I was delayed by private circumstances in coming to the house, and I bring it up to-night on its first call so that I may not lose the opportunity of presenting it.
By the Statute of Westminster we have become a nation, equal in partnership, of the commonwealth of the British Empire; we have ceased to be a dominion in order to become an independent nation under the sovereignty of the King of Great Britain, Ireland and the dominion beyond the seas. Having outgrown the status of a dominion, according to our. constitution, we are certainly not a republic-and may I add, I thank God we are not-we are a country which is under the sovereignty of King George Y and his successors. This country since the Treaty of France in 1763 has become one of the jewels, may I say, of the British crown. Having outgrown the status of a colony, not being a republic, we are, according to our constitution, according to history, according to facts, a country which is under the monarchical system, which has at its head a king or monarch and which is legislated for by him through a parliament, comprising the Senate, which takes the place of the House of Lords in England, and our House of Commons. Having ceased to be a dominion, having ceased to be a colony, not being a republic, we are therefore in our constitution a kingdom, and I claim that it is high time we should come back to the thought of the fathers of confederation and give to our country as its official name that of Kingdom of Canada.
In 1864, at the conference of Quebec, it was decided by the fathers of confederation that the new British-American state which was being created on the North American continent should be a kingdom. It was so officially styled in a draft which was submitted to the House of Commons in Great Britain. History tells us that the British House of Commons, or the minister for the colonies of the time, to please our republican friends to the south, decided to change the name to "Dominion of Canada" instead of "Kingdom of Canada," as was desired by Macdonald, Cartier, Galt and all the other fathers of confederation. In my opinion this was a mistake. It was unfortunate, but at the same time there was not only the fear of the republican sentiment of our neighbours to the south, but also the fear of displeasing, as making for independence the

Kingdom oj Canada-Mr. LaVergne
rabid imperialists who then lived in Canada. It was stated at the time that an independent or another kingdom under the British crown could not exist, as such a course would be contrary to logic, the fact being forgotten that for a long time the king of Great Britain had been King of Great Britain and, before the union of 1603, King of Great Britain and Scotland; King of Great Britain and Ireland; King of Great Britain, Ireland and France; King of Great Britain, Ireland, France and Hanover, until the Salic law prevented Queen Victoria from becoming Queen of Hanover. We have seen the joint kingdom of Sweden and Norway. Perhaps the house will permit me to refer to a letter written by Sir John A. Macdonald to Lord Knutsford on July 18, 1889, in which he says:
The union was treated by them-
That is, the House of Commons and House of Lords in Great Britain.
-as if the British North America Act were a private bill uniting two or three English parishes. Had a different course been pursued -for instance, bad united Canada been declared to be an auxiliary kingdom, as it was in the Canadian draft of the bill-I feel sure (almost) that the Australian colonies would, ere this, have been applying to be placed in the same rank as "the Kingdom of Canada."
And he added a postscript:
On reading the above over, I see that it will convey the impression that the change of title from Kingdom to Dominion was caused by the Duke of Buckingham.
The Duke of Buckingham at the time was Minister for the Colonies.
This is not so. It was made at the instance of Lord Derby, then Foreign Minister, who feared the first name would wound the sensibilities of the Yankees. I mentioned this to Lord Beaeonsfield at Hughenden in 1878, who replied: "1 was not aware of the circumstance, but it is so like Derby, a very good fellow but one who lives in a region of perpetual funk."
Therefore, if our country in 1867 was not called the Kingdom of Canada, it was for those two reasons which seem antagonistic but which we often find in combination in our history-the rabid imperialists on one side and those who 'have, to use the words of Lord Beaeonsfield, "a funk" of the Yankees.
Since by the Statute of Westminster we have acquired a status of equal partnership, it is high time that we should recognize our independence, our real status of equality, the system which administers our country, and that, having ceased to be a dominion, we should be called the Kingdom of Canada. By taking this course, we should at the same time do away with the title of the governor general; we are governing ourselves and it would follow logically that the governor general who
represents in this country the King of Great Britain and of Canada, should be a viceroy. If this house will look into the history of the resolution passed by the conference of 1864 it will find that the fathers of confederation intended to have as the chief executive in Canada the King of England or as a representative one of the members of the royal family.
I have given the reasons for the resolution and have outlined the historical facts. There is one other point upon which I should like to 'be perfectly frank. In this twentieth century, particularly since the great war, we have seen thrones crumbling and frenzied democracy asserting itself. I speak on behalf of a race which has had only one motto since it has been known as the French race,-God and the king. I feel that a voice should come from the true American continent asserting the undoubted benefits of the monarchical system, recognizing at the same time the proud state which our country has attained. I feel that we should no longer be a dominion, no longer a crown colony or one administered by the Governor General, but a free nation in the British commonwealth known as the Kingdom of Canada under the sovereignty of the King of Great Britain, Canada, Ireland and the other kingdoms of the empire.

Mr. Speaker, before this resolution comes to a vote, and as there appears to be a dearth of speakers on a motion of such importance as this one which concerns our country's name,. I should like to say a few words extempore in praise of the name of our country, the Dominion of Canada. Probably it will be easier for me to make these remarks than certain other hon. members-and I say this without intention of offence-because an hon. member might ordinarily be censured for what might appear to be disloyalty if he ventured to speak against a motion of this kind. I imagine, however, that a man who bore arms in support of his country and of his king is not liable to that criticism.
Some years ago, if my memory serves me correctly, I wondered just, how the Dominion of Canada acquired its name. I learned that while the fathers of confederation were debating what name they should give our country one of the fathers whose habit it was to read the scriptures before retiring happened to read one of the psalms, the following verse of which struck his imagination: "He shall have dominion also from sea to sea and from the river unto the ends of the earth." It was because of that biblical expression, Mr. Speaker, that the Dominion of Canada was named. Against the resolution of my hon. friend, the Deputy Speaker, I urge that the 
sacred and historic character of our nature is enshrined in the word "dominion" more than it ever can be in the word "kingdom." There is perhaps another reason. Since the Statute of Westminster, and even before that date, the self-governing units of the empire have been referred to as the self-governing dominions. And I believe they have been so called, because that word has been used to denote not only our connection with the empire but our autonomy. That is another reason why we should continue to adhere to and hold dear the name "Dominion of Canada."
I did not expect that this resolution would come before the house this evening. I rather feel that on a matter of this kind, which is perhaps one of high policy, one on which many hon. members of this house would want to take time to deliberate, it would perhaps be in order if I moved the adjournment of the debate, and I do so move, seconded by the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. B. M. Stitt).

maintopic: INTEREST ON BEARER BONDS-PROPOSED COLLECTION BY DEDUCTION OP TAX ON PAYMENT OF COUPONS
speechtext:
Whereas the question of securing proper returns from taxpayers so that no revenue properly taxable is to escape taxation becomes of utmost importance, especially in times of decreasing revenues such as at present;
Whereas the securing of revenue from these sources is difficult inasmuch as bonds to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars have been issued by the dominion and provincial governments as well as industrial companies, power and public utilities companies, the majority of these being bearer bonds transferable by delivery pass from hand to hand without any available record as to who holds them at any particular time.
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, legislation should be introduced providing that banks, trust companies and other agents in making payment of -interest coupons on bearer bonds shall deduct from the amount of each coupon the tax returnable to the federal or provincial governments interested and be responsible for the deposit of -the same in the federal or provincial treasury.
He said: The resolution, as I see it, speaks for itself. I am not offering any criticism; I am offering what I consider a practical suggestion that- will in my opinion result in the return to the federal and provincial exchequers of large amounts of taxes that have been missed. The honest man, of course, will make his return, but unfortunately we have others, and there is -the danger that we are losing a lot of money in this way. It would be a very

Redistribution-Mr. Barrette
simple matter, in my opinion, to tighten up the regulations or introduce some new system so that there would be no possible chance of the treasury losing taxes due from those who are well able to pay.
One thing we must bear in mind; we must take care of the small investors, those whose revenue is exempt. If this tax is collected at the source and the small investor is compelled to pay it, then there would have to be some way of rebating it to those who come under the exemption.
I think this resolution should have the unanimous support of the house.
Hon. E.N. RHODES (Minister of Finance): With the principle of this resolution the government is in entire accord; we have complete sympathy with the object sought to be attained. We have no hesitancy in accepting the resolution, although I may point out that while accepting the principle in its entirety there may have to be some variation from the procedure outlined. This resolution provides that the tax shall be deducted when the individual coupon is cashed. In numerous instances such bonds are in the hands of small holders by whom there is no tax payable, and to make the deduction at the source would involve such individuals in hardships and delay waiting for the cumbersome machinery of government to move before receiving their rebate, which in the nature of things might have to be many weeks or perhaps months. A better method, one which I think can be equally effective, is that of keeping absolute check upon the cashing of each individual coupon; then as it is disclosed that the coupon in question ought to bear a tax, the assessment can be made and the money returned to the treasury. This method would not only avoid the necessity of making refunds but would also save a large sum in accounting costs, and inconvenience to the treasury.
As I have already intimated to the house, before this session closes a measure will be brought down which I think will completely and effectively carry out the object of this resolution.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: PEOPOSED BASIS ON UNIT OF POPULATION OF PROVINCE OF ONTARIO
PEOPOSED BASIS ON UNIT OF POPULATION OF PROVINCE OF ONTARIO
speechtext:
Whereas this house will soon be called upon to effect a redistribution of electoral ridings in the various provinces constituting the Canadian confederation;
Whereas; the number of electoral ridings in each province other than the province of Quebec is based on the population unit of this latter province; and,
Whereas; the parliamentary representation of the province of Quebec with a population of 2,874,255 comprises 65 members, or a quotient of 44,219 per unit of representation; and,
Whereas; the parliamentary representation of the province of Ontario now comprises 82 members, with a population of 41,849 per unit of representation; and,
Whereas; notwithstanding the fact the population of the province of Ontario shows an increase in numbers but a decrease proportionally to the increase in the population of the province of Quebec, the latter province taking as a basis the unit of representation of the province of _ Ontario would be entitled to 69 members, New Brunswick 12. Manitoba 17, Saskatchewan 22, Alberta, 18, British Columbia 17;
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, in order to promote harmony among the Canadian people, the parliament of Canada do grant to the provinces a just and equitable representation based on the unit of representation of the province of Ontario.
Mr. Speaker, the resolution which the house is called upon to consider tends to do justice to the provinces which have not their fair quota of representatives in this parliament. I am broaching a rather ticklish question. It should give rise to quite an important debate in the house, as all hon. members are interested in rightly representing their province and exacting the largest representation possible so as to assert their rights. The purport of this resolution is to prove to the house that the province of Quebec has not, at present, the quota of representation to which it is entitled according to the last census.
Ever since confederation, the representation of each province has been based upon the representation of the province of Quebec. Each had the number of members to which it was entitled taking as a unit the population represented by each of the sixty-five members of Quebec, the decennial census was to be the basis of reckoning.
According to the last census, the province of Ontario should be deprived of four seats, if Quebec is taken as the unit of representation, but if Ontario retains its eighty-two seats, Quebec should be given sixty-nine instead of sixty-five, if we wish to place Quebec on the same footing as Ontario. In claiming these eighty-bwo seats. Ontario bases it>s contention on section 51, subsection 4 of the British North America Act, which reads as follows:
On any readjustment the number of members for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of the province bore to the number of the aggregate population of Canada at the then

Redistribution-Mr. Barrette
last preceding readjustment of the number of members for the province is ascertained at the then latest census to be diminished by one-twentieth part or upwards.
That is equivalent to a loss of 5 per cent in the ratio of its population.
The number of members of the House of Commons may be from time to time increased by the parliament of Canada, provided the proportionate representation of the provinces prescribed by this act is not thereby disturbed.
It is with reference to this article that I shall base my contention that Quebec be given sixty-nine members and that the other provinces be given the representation in the same ratio. I shall point out to the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) that, were he to accept my resolution, his province would be given three more members, Alberta, which is represented in the house by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), would have two more members, and Saskatchewan one more. Would any one oppose this resolution simply because Quebec would be entitled to four more representatives? I do not think that this would be a good reason for rejecting the resolution which I have the honour to submit to the consideration of the house.
When confederation was decided upon, this case was particularly dealt with by the fathers of confederation and a long debate ensued on this point, Sir Henri Joly de Lot-biniere had foreseen the situation which presents itself to-day. If you will permit me, I shall read to the house an excerpt of the discussion which then took place. In the Hansard of 1865, at pages 359 and 360, you will note, sir, that the Fathers of Confederation attached great importance to this question.
The following are the clauses of the resolution of the Quebec Conference which settles the organization of the House of Commons, especially as regards the number of representatives :
17.	The basis of representation in the House of Commons shall be population, as determined by the official census every ten years, and the number of members at first shall be 194, distributed as follows:
Upper Canada, 82.
Lower Canada, 65.
Nova Scotia, 19.
New Brunswick, 15.
Newfoundland, 8.
Prince Edward Island, 5.
18.	Until the official census of 1871 has been made up, there shall be no change in the number of representatives from the several sections.
19.	Immediately after the completion of the census of 1871, and immediately after every decennial census thereafter, the representation from each section in the House of Commons shall be readjusted on the basis of population.
20.	For the purpose of such readjustment, Lower Canada shall always be assigned 65

members, and each of the other sections shall at each readjustment receive, for the ten years then next succeeding, the number of members to which it will be entitled on the same ratio of representation to population as Lower Canada will enjoy according to the census last taken by having sixty-five members.
21.	No reduction shall be made in the number of members returned by any section, unless its population shall have decreased, relatively to the population of the whole union, to the extent of five per centum.
22.	In computing at each decennial period
the number of members to which each section is entitled, no fractional parts shall be considered, unless when exceeding one-half the number entitling to a member, in which case a member shall be given for each such fractional part.	.
I object, says "Sir Henri Joly de Lotbimere to the 21st clause, because it contains provisions which are unjust to Lower Canada. The full scope of that clause is not generally understood; that proportion of five per cent appears to be a very small affair, and yet, under certain circumstances, it might produce considerable results, which are not taken into consideration in the explanations given on that subject in the work written by the Hon. Mr. Cauchon, which the government has caused to be distributed (pages 72 to 87). It is difficult to foretell what the exact numerical increase of the several provinces will be from the present time to the next census in 1871. The Hon. Mr. Cauchon assumes, as the basis of his calculations, a rate of thirty per cent. Let us suppose the case to prove that in all the provinces (with the exception of Lower Canada) the population increases by thirty per cent between 1861 and 1871, and that of Lower Canada increases by thirty-four per cent. It may, perhaps, be objected to this that it is improbable. My reply is, that when we are discussing a scheme of such importance as that which is now under our consideration, we should provide for all possible contingencies; but this one is far from being impossible if the predictions of the Minister of Finance and the Attorney General, who promise to Lower Canada so brilliant a future under the federal system, are fulfilled. If Lower Canada become' the heart of the commercial life; if the mines of copper, lead, silver, and gold which we have lately discovered should produce the same results that they produce everywhere else, that of attracting a great influx of population, I cannot be accused of any great exaggeration in supposing that the population of Lower Canada may, between the years 1861 and 1871, increase by four per cent more than the population of the other provinces. In the case which I have supposed the increase would be as follows:

Upper Canada	 418,827
Lower Canada	 377,625
Nova Scotia	 99,257
New Brunswick	 75,614
Newfoundland	 [DOT]	39,000
Prince Edward Island	 24,227
Total increase	 1,034,550
According to this calculation, Lower Canada would have in 1871, a population of 1,488,289 souls, which would have to be divided by 65, that being the invariable number of representatives assigned to Lower Canada, in order to ascertain what would be the number of con-

Redistribution-Mr. Barrette
stituents for each representative in the federal parliament. The result will be found to be 22,896. Upper Canada would have a population of 1,814,918 souls, which, divided by 22,896 would give her 79 representatives instead of 82. Nova Scotia would have a population of 430,114 souls, which wrould give her 19 representatives as at present (eighteen and a fraction over the half). New Brunswick would have a population of 327,661 souls, which -would give her fourteen representatives instead of fifteen. Newfoundland would have a population of 169,000 souls, which would give her seven representatives instead of eight. Prince Edward Island would have a population of 104,984 souls, which would give her five members as at present (i.e. four and a fraction over the half). It would be seen that if the five other provinces were represented on the same scale as Lower Canada, they would, in 1871, lose among them five members; but as the total population of each will not have decreased by five per cent, relatively to the total population of the confederated provinces, there will be no reduction in the number of their representatives, in accordance with the provisions of this twenty-first clause. It is the interest of Lower Canada, more than any other province, to watch with a jealous eye over the mechanism adopted for the organization of the federal legislature. In case of a vital question arising, we should have to counteract the votes of these five members (who ought, in justice, to be deducted ipom the representation of the other provinces) by those of five of our members, whose votes would thus be lost to us, as would also be the weight which their five united counties, with a total population of 114,480 (or 22,896 for each county), would throw into the scale.
As you will note, Mr. Joly complained then of what is happening to-day. But Sir Hector Langevin, one of the fathers of confederation, pointed out to him that he misinterpreted the Confederation Act, and I am quoting an extract from his speech of February 21, 1865, page 391, of the Debates of the House of Commons of that day.
The hon. member for Lotbiniere, getting over his fears and predictions and speaking of the sixty-five members from Lower Canada, put the following question-"Suppose the papulation in Lower Canada should in ten years increase thirty-four per cent, while that of the other provinces increases only thirty per cent, would it not be unjust to Lower Canada that the number of its representatives should remain the same, should still be sixty-five, while that of the other provinces will be increased; while in any case the number of representatives from the provinces is not to be diminished unless their population should diminish five per cent?" This point is very important, but we must observe that whatever the increase of the population in the other provinces, the part from Lower Canada is fixed and known. Thus, for instance, if the population of Upper Canada should increase more than that of Lower Canada, the latter would always have sixty-five members, the other provinces receiving such increased number of representatives as their increased population would entitle them to. But the resolutions do not prevent Lower Canada from having more than sixty-five representatives, if its population should increase faster than that
of the other provinces. You will notice that in 1971, the Ontario population shall be slightly less than that of Quebec, nevertheless that province shall have retained its 82 members as against 65 from Quebec. In 1971, Ontario shall be assigned one member for a population of 66,177 while Quebec shall have one member for a population of 85,600, a difference of 19,423 per county, which nullify 1,262,495 votes from the latter province and 3,059,637 from all over Canada.
This proportion is absolutely ridiculous, in fact so much so that it makes it obvious that section 52 has been inserted to correct section 51 which is solely a clause to guarantee a certain minimum representation to the province.

If Ontario is to be allowed 82 members without increasing the representation of the other provinces, then the result will be that each member from Ontario will represent 41,856 constituents as against 44,219 for every member from the other provinces, (except Prince Edward Island) a difference of 3,269 constituents per county, which would make a total of 212,485 constituents whose votes would be nullified in Quebec only, or a total of 519,771 for the whole of Canada.
The British North America Act is the result of an agreement signed by the delegates from the several provinces of the Dominion, the basis of which being that every province shall be represented in the House of Commons by a number of members proportionate to its population. Every province had insisted on this condition and this is precisely why Prince Edward Island remained out of the confederation at the start.
[Mr. Barrette.!
The idea of confederation originated in Ontario, the most powerful of all provinces of the dominion, which for years had requested the representation by population.
Subsection 4 of article 51, was inserted with a view to the protection of the smaller provinces, and it never occurred to any of the delegates at the time that this clause might some day, serve to give the larger province of the dominion such a considerable advantage over the other provinces.
The population of Ontario which is affected by subsection 4 of section 51-that is to say one-twentieth of its comparative population, is four times more considerable than that of the second largest province-exception being made of Quebec-and thus give her a protection four times greater.
Parliament has not only the power but it has also the duty to carry out the provisions of section 52 of the act with a view to the re-adjustment of the representation from the provinces so that Ontario shall not be assigned a higher percentage of the membership of the house than her population entitles her to get and this can only be done by increasing the total membership of the house. Ontario has the right to retain her 82 members but the other provinces have also the right to an increased membership.
According to the census of 1931, Ontario has a population of 3,431,683 which if divided by 82 gives a result of 41,849; the population of the dominion is 10,374,196 from which we should deduct the population of Prince Edward Island, the Yukon and the North West Territories, which are assigned 5 members irrespective of population numbers 100,720 and therefore the net population of the other provinces, amount to 10,273,476, which divided by 41,849 would give 245 members for these provinces, and to that number should be added 2 members to provide for subsection 3 of section 51 which allow an extra member to a province for a fractional part exceeding one-half of the unit of representation and this would bring the total membership to 252 members including the five members for Prince Edward Island and the Yukon. Therefore, in all fairness to five provinces of the dominion a bill should be passed by the house stating that:-
"According to section 52 of the confederation act, the number of members of the House of Representatives is thereby increased from 245 to 252-and, the next House of Commons shall be constituted as prescribed by the confederation act upon the basis of repre-

And for this purpose subsection (1) of section 51 is changed to read:	"Quebec shall have
the fixed number of 69 members," and subsection 2 of section 51, is amended by substituting-"Number sixty-(five by number sixty-nine."
Section 52 gives to the Parliament of Canada the right to amend section 51-as mentioned above, as otherwise, Parliament could not take advantage of Section 52, as the number of members is controlled by the population of the Dominion divided by the population of Quebec multiplied by 65-plus such additional numbers guaranteed to the provinces by suib-Tsection 4 of section 51, and a special act of the Imperial Parliament which guarantees to each province as many members as they have senators.
It is therefore, very clear that unless the Parliament of Canada can increase the representation of Quebec it cannot take advantage of section 52 and this would be an absurdity.
I must point out that section 52 gives to parliament the right to increase the miemiber-shilp of the house but does not give it the right to reduce such membership. This reduction can only come in the natural operation of section 51 by an excess increase in the population of Quebec over the population of the other provinces. And this is an additional proof that the legislators intend to fix the representation of Quebec at 65 as a minimum and not as a maximum, as stated by Sir Hector Langevin.
What objections can there be to give to Quebec and five other provinces the increased membership they are entitled to receive? Economy? The indemnity of the 9 new members will total $28,000 less 10% or $25,800. By decreasing the indemnity of each member by 12i% instead of 10%, you will offset this increase in our expenditures and even if the full amount of $28,000 had to be provided for, the principle involved is worth much more as the advantages given to Ontario now represent the disfranchising of 212,485 of Quebec citizens, figure which is obtained by multiply-53719-117J
ing by 65 the difference of the unit of representation between Ontario and Quebec; each member represents 54,219 citizens in Quebec and only 41,850 in Ontario a difference of 3,269 by county. Also, you must keep in mind that at the time of confederation the unit of representation was 17,101 and it is, now 44,219, or more than 2i times greater. This unit should be stabilized around 40,000 and this can only be done by increasing the membership of the House.
If it does not take this logical and just action, the government will be facing a worse situation at the next census. During the next decade, indications show that Quebec and the West will continue to increase at a greater rate than Ontario. If the same rate prevailed, Ontario who has retained 1 seat more than she was entitled in 1921, and 4 seats more in 1931 would be entitled in 1941 to 8 seats less which she may keep on account of subsection 4 of section 51: in 1951, she will again keep 12 seats more than she is entitled, in 1961, 15 seats more and 1971, 19 seats more with the result that in 1971, with a population less than Quebec, Ontario would still retain its 82 members, against the 65 members of Quebec. Do you think that Quebec and the other provinces would tolerate this?
I fail to see how Ontario could be allowed to retain the representation it now enjoys without increasing proportionately the representation of the other provinces. The confederation act does not only permit but implicitly compels the house in this case to increase the membership of the house by using section 52 of the act. The rights of five provinces are involved and surely these five provinces should vote unanimously in favour of my resolution which is a recogniza-tion of their rights. A vote against it by any member of the province affected can only mean that this particular member would deliberately refuse to accept an increased membership for his province, because it would benefit Quebec too much. But this cannot be the spirit of justice which animated the present parliament and I expect that every member of this house will vote for my resolution as soon as he will stop to think and recognize its justification.
This resolution is of the utmost importance to the Province of Quebec, which would entitle it to four more members; British Columbia, so well represented by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), would be entitled to three more seats; Alberta to two, and Saskatchewan to one.
I do not see why, those who have an interest in setting forth the claims of their

respective provinces should not take advantage of the present resolution. In my own province it may be contended that it is simply a question of delivering a speech in the House and being placed in the limelight, however, I state the province of Quebec, under the circumstances, is entitled to have four more members, comparatively to the population of Ontario; this is what I am claiming at present in the house and I trust that my voice will be re-echoed, especially on this side of the house. I see by my side the honourable member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon), the honourable member for Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne) as well as the honourable member for St. Ann (Mr. Sullivan) all of whom, I am certain, will claim what is due to the province of Quebec. I am also aware that a number of my colleagues on your left, sir, will equally do their duty and claim for our province a just share of representation. I feel confident that the government will agree that the claim which I have just presented is just and will be favourably considered.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
I have not been able to
follow the hon. member for Berthier (Mr. Barrette) in his argument, but I think I understand fairly well the chief points of the case he has presented. The hon. member suggests that because of the application of, shall I say the rules of the game, as set forth in the British North America Act, it so happens, that the unit of population of Quebec at the present time exceeds the number which is found by dividing the number of members for Ontario into the population of that province, and that possibly there has been something in the nature of unfairness to the other provinces of Canada. The hon. member has been good enough to Indicate that in my own province of British Columbia, if his system of allocation of members throughout Canada were adopted, we would have three additional members instead of two. However, this situation is covered by the British North America Act.
The first point which I would like to draw to the attention of my hon. friend is that the resolution which he proposes, no matter what treatment it may receive, cannot in any way affect the matter as it is determined by the British North America Act. Let me direct the attention of the house and my hon. friend to the terms of his resolution. It will be noted that he asks for two things, his first proposal being that the parliament of Canada shall grant the provinces "just and equitable representation." I shall deal with this point in a moment when I refer to the

British North America Act. He then asks that this representation be based upon the unit of population of the province of Ontario.
When the fathers of confederation dealt with this very difficult and complex matter they hit upon a system which has I think been recognized throughout the British Empire, and probably throughout the world, as a. unique and admittedly fair method of ascertaining the representation within a dominion such as Canada. Furthermore, the fathers of confederation, and particularly Cartier, who as one of the members of the government at the time played an important part in formulating this particular scheme, were highly commended for the solution which they had arrived at. Through all the succeeding years this has been looked upon as one of the outstanding achievements of confederation. May I point out to my hon. friend that were it possible to adopt his resolution, which it is not; were we able to achieve the objective which he desires, namely, that the unit of representation should be based upon the population of Ontario provided by its present number of members, it would take away from his own province what has always been looked upon as one of its finest, shall I say, elements in its association with confederation-the fixture of its representation at sixty-five members.
A safeguard.
In the case of the maritime provinces is the number of senators to which they are entitled not the basis on which the number of their members to this house is established?

No, my hon. friend is
referring to another point. What he refers to, I think, applies to Prince Edward Island, namely, that the number of members in the house shall in no case be less than the number of senators in the province.

Does that
apply only to Prince Edward Island?

It applies to any province, but it is actually in force only in regard to Prince Edward Island, because all the other provinces, I think without exception, have at the present time a larger number of members than senators.
The numbers are pretty close in New Brunswick.

Yes, they are getting
close. But the point I wish to make is that rule No. 4 of section 51 of the British North America Act has completely anticinated the

Redistribution-Mr. Stevens
very point he has raised-that is the main argument he advances-and has specifically provided for it. Consequently it is not competent for us to change that.
The hon. gentleman then proceeds to section 52, and under it he makes the claim that it is competent for the house to increase the number of members. I shall read section 52 and then indicate wherein I differ from my hon. friend in the interpretation of it. Section 52 reads:
The number of members of the House of Commons may be from time to time increased by the parliament of Canada, provided the proportionate representation of the provinces prescribed by this act is not thereby disturbed.
Obviously, the meaning of that section is simply that should, for instance, Quebec stand dormant, without increase in its population -a condition which, heaven knows, is impossible, but still let us assume for the sake of argument it were so-and the rest of Canada were to increase rapidly in population, then the unit of population ascertained by the division of the population of Quebec by sixty-five, divided into the rest of Canada, would very probably call for a much larger number of members than at present sit in the house. While the hon. member was speaking, I made a brief computation which will illustrate this point. Let us assume for the sake of argument that in the next decennial period the population of Quebec did not change and the number of members being sixty-five, the unit of population would be, as at present, 44,219. But assume also that
3,000,000 were added to the rest of Canada: that would give an additional 240 members above the number for Quebec, or, in all, 305 members who would have seats in the house. I admit that with the division of provinces there would be fractions which would vary that, but I am taking it just as a general argument. In other words, if the population of Canada outside Quebec increased at a more rapid ratio than did Quebec, there would be an increase of membership in the house. So the fathers of confederation, realizing that that might occur, provided that the parliament of Canada, in the event of such a happening, should have the power to increase the number of members in the house, and of course this has been done from time to time. I believe at the last decennial census it worked out that the increase was from 241 to 245 members. I am speaking from memory.
From 235 to 245.

I do not
rise to discuss the motion. I agree with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), that the representation as provided in the British North America Act has so far worked out very satisfactorily for all the provinces. But my friend and colleague, the exMinister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), expressed a desire to discuss this motion, and I would ask permission to adjourn the debate in order to give him an opportunity to speak to the motion later. I do not wish to cut off discussion now.

Mr. Speaker, I regret very much to occupy the time of the house and delay proceedings by a further discussion of this important matter, certain phases of which have been fully covered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). I am sorry also that my knowledge of the French language is not sufficient to have enabled me to follow the mover of the resolution (Mr. Barrette). After listening to the clear responses made by the minister, however, I believe I have a fair grasp of the pertinent portions of the mover's remarks. It would appear from what has transpired in the last few years that the farther we remove ourselves from the time of confederation, the farther we remove ourselves from the spirit and intentions of the fathers of confederation and get down to the strict and rigid interpretation of the British North America Act. I believe before I have concluded I shall have established to the satisfaction of hon. members the fact that at least in some measure that is so.
With the few minutes at my disposal I should like to give a brief history of the question of representation in this house as it affects the maritime provinces, and the inequalities with which we have had to contend for a great many years. Representation in this house is a burning question in the maritimes to-day on account of what would appear to be a further decrease in our representation in the near future, which we claim is already too greatly reduced.
A conference of the representatives of the provinces of Canada met in December, 1910, convened by the premiers of Ontario and Quebec, to consider the representation of the maritime provinces in the parliament of Canada. This question was discussed at considerable length, but no decision was reached.
A further conference was held in October, 1913, at Ottawa, to continue the study of the question of representation and other matters. A resolution was moved by the premiers of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island:
That, in the opinion of this conference, the representation granted to the maritime provinces at the time they respectively entered confederation should be restored and rendered irreducible.
After considerable debate, this resolution was withdrawn and another substituted to the effect that an amendment to the British North America Act be sought providing an irreducible minimum in the representation of the maritime provinces of eighteen for Nova Scotia, thirteen for New Brunswick and six for Prince Edward Island. This also was withdrawn, and a resolution dealing with the problem of Prince Edward Island was introduced. Finally, the conference passed the following:
Resolved, that this conference expresses the opinion that, not representing the provinces for the purposes of this matter of representation, it declines to take any action in regard to it.
At this conference two memoranda were presented, one by the premiers of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, and the other on behalf of Prince Edward Island, urging its special claim. At that time, 1913, as a result of the census of 1911, Nova Scotia's representation had been reduced from eighteen to sixteen, New Brunswick's from thirteen to eleven, and Prince Edward Island's from four to three. The representation of the western provinces had increased according to their population.
One result of the conference was an amendment to the British North America Act, 5-6 George Y, chapter 45, providing that " notwithstanding anything in the said act, a province Shall always be entitled to a number of members in the House of Commons not less than the number of senators representing such province." This enabled Prince Edward Island to retain a fourth member.
For a moment or two I should like to speak concerning what we claim is the loss of a federal member from the province of Nova Scotia, despite the present method of establishing the unit of representation for each of the provinces of Canada.
The population of Nova Scotia increased from 1911 to 1921 by 31,499, Quebec's population increased at a relatively larger rate, so that the unit of representation after the 1921 census became 36,283. Nova Scotia's representation in the House of Commons was therefore reduced from 16 to 14. The population contained 33,965 more than was necessary to give fourteen representatives, but because we had fallen 2,318 below the fractional part, not exceeding one-half of the whole number required to entitle the province to a member, our population to that
Redistribution-Mr. Smith

extent was disregarded, and we suffered the loss of one member. Nova Scotia could not
*'ain its members, as Ontario did, under subsection 4 of section 51 of the British North America Act, whereby no reduction can be made unless the proportion which the population of the province bears to the total population of the dominion be diminished by one-twentieth part or upwards.
It may be difficult to overcome an effect such as this, but it is a fact that there are 33,965 persons in Nova Scotia unrepresented in the House of Commons while there are in Canada, outside of the maritime provinces ninety-six electoral districts returning members with less than that population within their bounds. The membership for Nova Scotia cannot be reduced below ten, the number of our senators. But if by the increase of population in Quebec our representation were lowered to this minimum, it would mean a total reduction since confederation of nine. This is a condition which is being rapidly approached. Had the unit of representation, instead of being 36,283 been 36,125, a difference of 158, Nova Scotia would have been saved another representative, and instead of having fourteen members in the House of Commons would have had fifteen; that is, if the population of Quebec had been less by 10,287 persons the unit would have been so reduced.
By the British North America Act, section 51, subsection 2-
There shall be assigned to each of the other provinces such a number of members as will bear the same proportion to the number of its population (ascertained at such census) as the number sixty-five bears to the number of the population of Quebec (so ascertained).
Quebec is defined by this act, section 6 as follows:
The part of the province of Canada (as it exists at the passing of this act) which formerly constituted respectively the provinces of upper Canada and lower Canada, shall be deemed to be severed, and shall form two separate provinces. The parts which formerly constituted the province of upper Canada shall constitute the province of Ontario: and the part which formerly constituted the province of lower Canada shall constitute the province of Quebec.
That is, the population to be taken is the population of the territory known as Quebec at the passing of the British North America Act. But the population of Quebec which has been taken as the basis for the unit of representation since 1900 is the population of that province as originally constituted, plus the population of the extensions made by chapter 3 of the acts of 1898. It is now possible, from information at hand to ascertain just what population was counted in these added 
territorities, for they contain all of Abitibi, the district of Labrador, and what is known as part of east Maine, all that territory north of the height of land, part of it being traversed by the National Transcontinental Railway. In extending the boundaries further in 1912 the territory then given to Quebec was excluded in considering the population forming the unit of representation but the population added by the Act of 1898 is included. A statement from the dominion statistician shows that there were 13,644 people in this area. These should not have been counted in determining the unit of representation. Excluding them, the unit becomes not 36,283 as used, but 36,073. This figure divided into the population of Nova Scotia, 1921, gives 14 and a fractional part, exceeding one-half of the whole united number by 778 and entitling this province to another federal member. The representation in the House of Commons from Nova Scotia, as fixed by the Redistribution Act, 1924, should therefore have been fifteen members. The province was under-represented in the last parliament by one member and will be in the next unless immediate steps are taken to correct this error.
Now let me refer you to some remarks of the fathers of confederation. I begin with a statement by Sir John A. Macdonald in the parliamentary debate on confederation in 1865:
By adopting the representation of Lower Canada as a fixed standard-as the pivot on which the whole would turn-that province being the best suited for the purpose, on account of the comparatively permanent character of its population, and from its having neither the largest nor the least number of inhabitants.
But instead of the population of Quebec being "comparatively permanent" in its Character it has shown a relatively large increase and is overflowing into territory which did not form part of its original area. Taking the original provinces into consideration, Nova Scotia has increased in fifty years 35.8 per cent, New Brunswick, 35.2 per cent, Quebec, 98.17 per cent, and Ontario, 80.99 per cent. Quebec, therefore, has shown the largest relative percentage of increases of the four original provinces and is the least stable in character instead of being comparatively permanent.
Gray, in his account of the conference at Quebec, states:
Thus at the first inception on entering into the union, population was not intended to be held as the only rule for representation. Though taken as a guide, the apportionment must be more or less arbitrary. Existing arrangements. territorial and other considerations must be taken into account, and modifications to suit

Redistribution-Mr. Smith
circumstances necessarily made; but after entering the union, future changes of the entire representation were to be governed by that principle. .	. The conference, therefore, while
taking population as the basis, and laying down that strictly as the rule, acted upon the principle that in the first instance territorial area and local circumstances must also be considered.
The memorial which was presented at the interprovincial conference in 1913 on behalf of the three maritime provinces forms substantially their claims to-day. The memorial reads:
The question of the legal right of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island to retain their original representation was referred to the Supreme Court of Canada in 1903, and was decided against these provinces. On appeal to the privy council the answer of the supreme court to the question submitted was held to be correct.
We must bow to this decision so far as the strict interpretation of the written contract is concerned, but this was not the expectation and belief of the delegates at the time of the negotiations of the terms of union, for the Honourable George Brown, in moving the resolution fixing the number of representatives which each colony should have in the house, stated: "The practical result will be that while Lower Canada certainly will not be less and the lower provinces may increase in population, they cannot decrease in the number of representatives. It keeps the bouse within a reasonable limit."
And in a speech delivered at Sherbrooke in 1864, shortly after the Quebec conference, Hon. A. T. Galt had said:
We have supposed that the population of Lower Canada, being tolerably equable in its character, would afford the best basis. But having respect to the rapid increase of Upper Canada, we think the lower provinces should not be reduced if they do not increase in the same ratio. Therefore, the lower provinces would have the same as they have now unless in the very improbable case of any one falling off by five per cent or more-that is, a decrease relatively to the whole federation.
Representation by papulation, while accepted as a guiding principle in fixing the representation of each province, in the dominion parliament, was intended to be made subservient to the right of each colony to adequate representation in view of its surrender of a large measure of self-government. In consideration of surrendering its independent colonial status, each colony was entitled to such a representation in the federal parliament as would be sufficient to guard that right.
A self-governing colony wras something more than the number of its habitants.
The principle that population was not the sole consideration in fixing representation was recognized in the cases of Manitoba, British Columbia and Prince Edward Island when these provinces respectively entered the union.
Manitoba, with a population less than one unit of representation, was given four, with a provision that after the census of 1881 its representation should be "readjusted" under the terms of the British North America Act.
The census of 1881 showed a population of sixty-two thousand two hundred and sixty,
which would have entitled it to three members, but it was "readjusted" up to five.
British Columbia with a white population of less than ten thousand and a total population not exceeding forty thousand when it entered Confederation, in 1871, was given six members as an irreducible minimum. In 1881 it had but two units of representation and in 1891 four units.
Prince Edward Island obtained six members upon entering confederation with but five units of population, passed the census of 1881 in the same condition, but, not being safeguarded as was British Columbia, was reduced to a representation of five after the census of 1891.
It may be said that in each of these cases there was an expectation of such increase as would in time bring all the provinces upon the basis of representation allowed upon entering confederation. Admitting such to be the case, it goes to show that the splendid optimists who made confederation thought only of readjustment upwards and not downwards.
When the maritime provinces entered confederation it was impossible for them to have foreseen the extent and effect of the development of western Canada. They never imagined that in the days to come the growth of the west would strip them of their influence in the councils of the nation. Though the times were not over prosperous, they contributed their share to the cost of purchasing the lands from the Hudson Bay Company and equipping them for 'settlement; bore their part of the cost of Canada to the Canadian Pacific Railway and all the other vast expenditures that went to link together the far-flung provinces of Canada and to convert the wilderness into thriving communities out of which have developed the splendid prairie provinces of to-day. But most of all, they gave their sons and daughters to the ivest. From Manitoba to the Pacific coast the maritime provinces people form an important element of the population who have played no small part in the development of these new lands.	. .
All these contributions the maritime provinces have cheerfully made in the interests of Canadian unity and progress: but they feel it a cruel exaction of the strict letter of the bond which will impose a lasting penalty upon them for the sacrifices they have made in such a cause.
I appeal to this house, Mr. Speaker for unity and justice in this matter. This resolution may not be the appropriate time to express our views on this question, but as it would appear that this may be the last opportunity to present our case before the redistribution bill is brought into the house and passed I appeal to this parliament for a spirit of unity and fair play with respect to the representation of the maritime provinces in this house which has suffered so badly. I feel that we have every just right to put forward this claim, which I have humbly endeavoured to do in the interest of the province from which I come.

I think it is becoming apparent that the existing representation of the province of Quebec in
Redistribution-Mr. Cardin

the House of Commons is not adequate, and that a change might be sought in the near future. I do not contend that the resolution which is undetr consideration is the proper mode of attaining that purpose. I admit quite frankly and without hesitation thait the argument of the Minister of Trade and Commerce appears to me to be perfectly correct and in accordance with the true interpretation of the statute. I do not think that the mover of the resolution (Mr. Barrette) had in mind changing the system of determining representation in the House of Commons; he only wanted to make an adjustment for the present owing to the inadequacy in practice of the British North America Act.
It is said that the representation has been settled as it now is with a view to providing a safeguard for the province of Quebec. It has turned out, however, that this safeguard has worked against the province of Quebec. The law has not fulfilled the expectations of the fathers of confederation, because at the present time the province of Quebec finds itself in an unfavourable position when that law is carried into practice. This is not the fault of an3rone in this house; it is the fault of the fathers of confederation, who made the mistake in making their estimation of what would be the result of their legislation and what the growth of population in the different provinces might be. One can readily understand that it is not fair that a member should represent a constituency in the province of Quebec on the basis of a population of 44,000 while a member representing a constituency in the province of Ontario does so on the basis of 41,000. As I have said, however, the remedy is not to be found in the resolution which has been presented to the house by the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge (Mr. Barrette). As has been said, when the redistribution bill was presented to the house, an amendment to the British North America Act would be required to achieve the aim of the hon. member, and I think the whole speech of the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge was based on a wrong interpretation of the British North America Act and of the resolutions passed in 1864 or 1865, as interpreted by Sir Hector Langevin. The true position was placed before the members at the time by Sir Henry Joly, and the argument made by him was perfectly correct and in accordance with the true interpretation of the resolutions and of the different sections of the British North America Act. When Sir Hector Langevin undertook to reply to Sir Henry Joly and to try to dispel the fears he had expressed, Sir Hector
FMr. Cardin.]
Langevin was entirely wrong, and the text of the law would not justify the interpretation which he gave the resolutions at that time. Sir Hector Langevin had based his whole argument, in his reply to Sir Henry Joly, on section 52, which empowers parliament to increase the number of representatives of the different provinces; but the mistake he made was this, that section 52 could not be interpreted as a contradiction of section 51. Section 51, subsection 1, provided that Quebec should have a fixed number of 65 members. A fixed number of 65 members means that the number cannot be increased or decreased, and section 52 cannot be interpreted as meaning that the representation of the province of Quebec can be increased when section 51 declares that it cannot be increased and that the number of 65 members is fixed. The whole argument of the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge is based on the observations made at the time by Sir Hector Langevin, whose argument was based upon an error and a wrong interpretation, a supposed contradiction between section 52 and subseotion 1 of section 51. That is the whole question.
Apart from the question of law, I think it is well that all members of the house should keep in mind and give their best attention to the possibility of going into the matter on another occasion, with a view to providing for a change in the British North America Act, because, according to the calculation placed beifore the house, before very long there will arise a situation which will be unjust to the province of Quebec. I think it is the duty of all hon. members of this house, who are desirous of preserving that harmony that has always existed in the relationships of the citizens of the various provinces of Canada, to study this question seriously, and when the next opportunity presents itself to find a better and more equitable basis for representation of the province of Quebec in the House of Commons.
On motion of Mr. Stewart (Edmonton) the debate was adjourned.

PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF SPREAD BETWEEN PRICES OF RAW PRODUCTS AND MANUFACTURED GOODS
speechtext:
Thait, in the opinion of this house, an immediate inquiry should be made under the provisions of The Research Council Act, chapter 177, R.S.C., 1927, or by other means, into the

Production-Mr. McKenzie
causes underlying the wide spread between the prices of raw products and the prices of goods manufactured from such products.
He said: In presenting to the house the resolution which you have just read, Mr. Speaker, I do so because I am firmly convinced that in many instances an injustice is being perpetrated upon our people, which has the effect of bringing the present depression to bear more heavily than it need bear, particularly upon the farmers and the labouring classes. In the second place, I find that there is throughout the country a demand that the government provide means for the most effective relief possible by enabling the people to buy their necessities as Cheaply as they can, discarding all handicaps that have a tendency to make living expenses higher than they ought to be. In many instances our farmers and labouring classes particularly find the cost of living bearing more heavily upon them than it has ever done previously. This is due largely to the disastrous fall in prices in the last few years of those commodities which the primary producers have to sell in the markets of the world, and also the fact that there is not a similar decline in the prices of manufactured products.
I go to a relief officer in any part of the country and ask him about relief matters, and at once I am told that one of our greatest needs in relief work is clothing; and I ask myself why it is that clothing is so badly needed when all our products are at sudh low prices. The only answer I can make is that the price of clothing of all kinds is too dear when compared with the purchasing power of the individual. This fact is the reason for this resolution.
Some months ago I sent a letter to the weekly and daily press throughout Canada, almost from one end to the other, in which I drew attention to the wide spread between the price received by the farmer for his raw wool and the price he had to pay for underwear. I dealt with just that one article, but I received letters from people all over the country. At that time wool was selling at from four to four and one-half cents per pound and people were having to pay from $2 to $4 per pound for the same wool manufactured into underwear. From the many letters which I received I learned that there were many people like myself who were wondering why there was such a wide spread between the price received for raw wool and the price paid for the finished product. Many people had arrived at the same conclusion as myself, that someone was making a high profit. One man evidently had settled in his
own mind the reason for this wide spread; he seemed to have a solution, nevertheless it was hard for me to understand why four cent wool should become two, three and four dollar wool when manufactured into underwear. I have most of these letters before me and I shall give a few extracts to show the feelings of different people throughout the country in connection with this very matter.
One man wrote that he had purchased a pair of trousers for $10 the weight of which was two pounds. He said they were simply trash in comparison with trousers he had bought in Scotland for fifteen and sixteen shillings. I wonder why the imperial conference did not do something to enable the clothing manufacturers in the old land, who could produce at less than half the cost of the manufacturers in Canada, to send their goods into this country.
Another man wrote that his sheep were of the Rambouillet breed which produces a very fine grade of clothing wool. He received six cents per pound for this wool, a premium of one or two cents over the market price. He went out and bought three ounces of fine yam at twenty cents per ounce; in other words, he exchanged ten pounds of wool for three ounces of yarn. That would seem to explode the argument that high wages is the reason for this spread, because we know that wages make up only a small part of the cost of converting raw wool into yarn.
Another man wrote and said that four years ago he had bought one hundred per cent woollen underwear for $3.50 per suit; at that time he had sold his wool for twenty-five cents per pound, but this year while he had to pay the same price for his underwear he could get only four and one-eighth cents per pound for his wool.

speechtext:
The hon.
member will have a chance to explain, if he wishes. He is not from western Canada, and this letter was received from a resident in that part of the country. '
Production-Mr. McKenzie

Another man sent me a purchase slip covering two suits of underwear at $2.95 per suit, their weight being thirteen ounces. This would show t/hat the wool in the manufactured state was selling at over $3 per pound.
All this was a year ago; but let us see what the conditions are to-day. I say to my hon. friend that they are very much worse to-day than they were a year ago. A farmer in my own part of the province of Saskatchewan sent 600 pounds of wool to Winnipeg through the cooperative organization and at the same time ordered some blankets, the cost of which was to be charged against his wool. To his surprise he received word that bis wool was too dark in colour and that owing to the deplorable state of the market no advance could be made on his shipment either in cash or in credit. That is the condition which exists today. When I received these letters raw wool was selling at four or five cents per pound, but to-day some of our farmers are receiving only two and two and a half cents per pound. The relief officers still report that the greatest need of the people to-day is clothing, and the price of this manufactured product is very little below what it was three or four years ago when the farmers were receiving twenty-five cents per pound for their wool.
I am frequently asked whether conditions in western Canada are better to-day than they were last year. Last year if you spoke to almost any farmer in western Canada about the conditions which prevailed he replied that things would not be too bad, even with the low prices, provided he could get a good crop; he felt that he would be able to pull through. Taken on the whole, the crop in western Canada was quite good; in some parts of my province it ran forty to forty-five bushels per acre in wheat, but because of the prices he received for his crop the farmer is even poorer to-day as far as money is concerned than he was a year ago. It is true that there is plenty of food for everybody, but money is out of the question.
Last year our people were hoping that the imperial conference would surely do something to relieve conditions, that it would permit the good quality clothing which is produced at lower prices in the old country to come into Canada, the type of clothing so badly needed by the people of this country. This conference, to say the least, has gone into the limbo of forgotten things, with no benefits so far to our farmers. Even the preference on wheat and the bacon quota have been of no value whatever to them.
In the replies which I received to the letters which I sent to the press, I was quite frequently

asked: Why do you mention wool? A man from British Columbia would say: Conditions are just as bad with regard to our fruit, our fisheries, and people in other parts of the country would mention other products in regard to which they said the situation was just as bad as that of wool. My reason for mentioning wool was that in Saskatchewan, the province from which I come, during the hard winters which we have there, people require woollen clothing and they find it almost impossible to buy it at the prices which prevail. That is why I said that wool was too cheap, while on the other hand woollen clothing was too dear.
Let me put the situation in this way. In western Canada to-day we have farmers who do not shear their sheep because it does not pay them to do so, especially if they have to hire a man to shear them; the wool will not pay for the cost of shearing. On the other hand, those farmers and their families are not able to buy woollen clothing because it is too dear. Under such conditions I say to the government that something must foe done. Surely they will not permit such a situation to continue without endeavouring to do something towards relieving it.
My resolution, however, does not deal with wool alone; it deals with products in general, and I have no douibt some adjustment is just as urgent in many other lines. In fact, I have with me newspaper clippings indicating that many other people are as firmly convinced as I am that there is a need for adjustment in many other lines. I have under my hand a clipping which I took from the Farmer's Sun of December 8 last, which says:
Farm price declines fail to aid consumer.
Burden of debt doubled, but, while producer gets less, distributors maintain same spread.
AH interests not bearing same burden.
Then the article goes on to show the spread between the price of wheat and the price of flour and bread. It deals also with something which is quite noticeable in the cities, and that is the difference between the price the farmer receives for his cattle and the prices people have to pay in city shops for their meat. It also mentions the high price of milk, retail, in comparison with what 'the farmer receives. Then it deals with another subject which was dealt with in a resolution introduced earlier to-day and which the government is evidently going to send to the banking and commerce committee. I refer to the question of the burden of debt. It says:
Farm prices have been cut in half.

That is hardly a correct statement, because they have been cut in three and in some oases even four.
Debts mortgages, interest rates, remain the same.
I believe the time has come when something must be done with regard to the question of debt and interest.
I have under my hand a clipping, a letter sent to the Winnipeg Free Press and signed by John Farmer of Sennett, Saskatohewan. I want to read a portion of it because it deals directly with the resolution which I am presenting. It appears in the issue of December 3, 1932. It is headed:
800 pounds of wheat for eight ounces of tin.
This gentleman says:
Since the imperial conference I have had occasion to order extra parts for a cream separator, which I have been using for the past 16 years. The parts required were a tin float, a tin cup, in which the float works, and three small rubber rings.
Not knowing the price of these articles I enclosed one dollar with my order, deeming it sufficient to pay for both extras and postage.
The articles ordered from a house in Winnipeg came by parcel post with a c.o.d. charge against them for $2.91. This amount, plus the dollar that I had sent with my letter, covered the cost of the goods and the postage and money order fee.
The total cost to me was almost four dollars. The two articles of tin, together, weighed exactly 8 ounces.
I understand that tin is a product of our own country, and taking this into consideration along with the current prices of the commodities that I had to sell in order to raise the money to pay for repairs for my cream separator, the following rather startling facts were revealed. At 30 cents a bushel, I would have to exchange 800 pounds of wheat for 8 ounces of tin; or 1,600 pounds of barley at 12 cents a bushel; or 1,700 pounds of oats at 8 cents a bushel; or 40 dozen of eggs at 10 cents a dozen; or 331 pounds of butter at 12 cents a pound. The labour and expense incidental to producing these commodities would, I think, more than offset the labour and expense of manufacturing a float and a cup out of 8 ounces of tin.
The prices quoted above were current at the time of ordering the separator parts, which was in the early part of October, 1932.
Examples of this kind should, I think, be brought forcefully to the attention of our government. Do they realize the weight of the unjust burden placed on the farmers while they are protecting the manufacturer?
Then the letter goes on to deal with the matter of protection about which I may have a little to Bay Later on.
Many anomalous conditions exist throughout the country. For instance, we have oats selling in Saskatchewan at seven cents a bushel and even lea?, but oatmeal is selling at five cents a pound. A naan would have to
Production-Mr. McKenzie
sell about thirty cow hides at present prices to buy one pair of cowhide boots. Wool is selling at about two cents a pound while underwear is in the neighbourhood of $3 a pound. Just consider the fact that a man would have to care for, house, feed and shelter the year round and shear, if he thought it was necessary, thirty sheep in order to get enough money from the wool to buy one suit of underwear. Surely that is a condition which ought not to be permitted to exist. A year ago I brought to the attention of the house another anomalous condition with regard to a man in western Canada who took a calf skin into a store where they gave him fifty cents for it. He bought a pair of shoelaces which cost him twenty cents, and a clerk in the store figured out that if he were to buy back that whole calf skin in the form of shoelaces, it would cost him something over S70. Surely that is a condition about which it should be possible to do something.
IV heat at present is selling retail at country elevators in western Canada at thirty cents a bushel, while puffed wheat is worth more than $30 a bushel. Surely something can be done in regard to such a situation. I believe the government are aware that something should be done in connection with this matter. I was pleased last year with the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture (Mi. Weir) when he spoke regarding agricultural conditions and the proposed appointment of a marketing board. His words appear at page 3400 of Hansard for 1932:
I assure hon. gentlemen that we have given more attention and thought to this question than to any other,-
Referring to the marketing board.
-and in this connection I have received excellent cooperation from hon. members irrespective of party. Because of the reasons I have stated it has been thought best to appoint a commission to study the whole problem of marketing, and the government intends to appoint such commission to study this question, especially in connection with export marketing. It will study the problem of supply and demand and perhaps more particularly the spread in the processing of the major farm products.
I regret the board has not been appointed, and particularly that no action has been taken concerning the last part of the minister's words I have just quoted. I have never been very much in favour of the marketing board, except in so far as it would have power to investigate these processing spreads. I want to emphasize again that something must be done; western Canada has practically reached the breaking point. People cannot go on this way very much longer. If in time of war it was necessary to create
Production-Mr. McKenzie

statutes preventing undue profits; why not do it now? I believe it is more necessary to-day than it was during war times.
I may be asked for my suggestion. I do not believe it necessary to make any. The resolution standing in my name states specifically that the matters to which I have referred should be placed in the hands of the body appointed for that particular purpose, namely for the purpose of investigating conditions such as these. The investigations could therefore be made without cost to the government. The research council has the power to make investigations and to summon any persons they may wish to give evidence before them. I know there are people who are satisfied that if we had proper tariff legislation-and I must confess I am one of them -conditions would be greatly improved. A reduction in tariffs would help to relieve matters. Others say we cannot have a proper adjustment unless there is greater control of currency. That is a factor which may be of importance. Then there are those who say that reduced tariffs and control of currency would be of no use unless an attempt were made to control the monopolies, combines and cartels which control industries to such an extent throughout the world. I do not know just to what extent industry is controlled by monopolies, but I am told that a large percentage of industries are to some extent under the control of monopolies or combines. Then there are others who say that the trouble lies in ineffective distribution and transportation, and that until these difficulties are corrected we cannot expect any relief. I would say that something must be done concerning the spread in prices, even though the government may find it necessary to take over industries, as some of our friends in the corner suggest. If it is necessary, let them do it. I am firmly convinced, however, that undue profits in all lines of industry must be curtailed, and that industrialists must not be allowed to charge more than reasonable profits.
