PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF SPREAD BETWEEN PRICES OF RAW PRODUCTS AND MANUFACTURED GOODS
speechtext:
There is an expression that I have used in this house on former occasions, taken from Bastiat, and I want to repeat it because it should be graven on the mind of every man in this house. It is this:
Study all economic questions from the consumers standpoint, for the consumers' interests are the interests of the human race.
Every improvement in the methods of production or distribution of goods should result in lower prices to the consumer. If it does so result it benefits the whole human race the consumer, which includes everybody, because he has more goods available for consumption; the producer, because he has more employment in producing that greater quantity of goods.
Let me give you an example. Take the printing industry. Prior to the invention of printing, the transcribing of the written word was a slow and laborious process, and not
Production-Mr. Young

many men were employed in it. Their work was physically painful; their wages were small, and very little reading matter was produced and made available to the people. Then someone invented printing. What was the result? Printed matter became so cheap, that the advantage of the new invention passed on to the consumer in the form of cheaper printed matter resulted in an ever greater and greater demand for the printed word. Instead of a few hundred men being employed in transcribing the written word thousands nay, millions of men were employed, and the wages they received were infinitely greater than the wages of the old-fashioned hand writers. People throughout the world were enlightened, received the benefits of knowledge, which can be traced directly to the invention of printing and the passing on to the consumer of the benefits of the invention. The men who profited by the process, although they made not nearly so much profi'; per written sheet, found their aggregate profits enormously greater than they otherwise would have been. Suppose those in charge of that industry had said: "We will not pass on this advantage to the consumer, we will appropriate to ourselves all the advantage of the new invention, charge as much as we ever did for the written page, and put the profit in our pockets,"-what would have been the result? No increased demand for printing, no increased number of people employed in the industry-a larger profit on each individual sheet to be sure, but the aggregate profits would not have been as a drop in the well compared with what they are to-day.
Take another example, the invention of the loom. Before the time of that invention cloth was made by a slow and laborious process requiring a great amount of human labour to produce it, so much, indeed, that people could not afford many clothes, and what they had were of the coarsest. Someone invented the loom. Those engaged in the industry, seeing this new machine coming and throwing them out of employment said, "This machine is going to take away our livelihood", and they proceeded to wreck the machines and had to be restrained by law. What happened? They soon discovered that the invention of this new process was cheapening the production of doth so that now everyone was buying cloth; the demand increased so enormously that more men than ever were employed in the industry. The benefit was passed on to the consumer. All humanity profited by the advantage of having cheaper clothing. Those engaged in the industry profited because they

had more work and better wages, and those who owned the industry found that their profits were greater in the aggregate, though they might be less on each piece of cloth. This, then, we can take as the rule: that wherever the advantage of an improvement in method or process of production or distribution is passed on to the consumer in the form of lower prices, all humanity benefits; but whenever an attempt is made to retain that advantage to one person or group of persons, whether capital or labour, whoever they may be, the result is less employment for the human race and nothing added to the aggregate wealth of the world.
Improvement should always result in lower prices. When an improvement in any process or the invention of a new machine does not result in lower prices, then one of two things is true: either that machine is not truly a labour-saving device, or somebody is taking too heavy a toll and profiteering by it. It is quite conceivable that a new machine or a new process of producing a certain article might be invented, and that the labour cost required to produce that machine might be greater than the labour saved by the use of it. But that does not often happen. Generally there is a real saving in labour, and unless it is passed on to the consumer in the form of lower prices, the result is less wealth for the human race, less employment, smaller profits for those interested in the industry, and more misery in the world.
To-day the tendency throughout the world is to keep prices up. Whenever any institution or industry installs new machinery or improves its processes, the last thing they think of is passing the benefit on to the consumer; they want to retain it to themselves; and in order to conceal their profits, as my hon. friend from Last Mountain has said, they call in the high financier. They water their stock and expect the industry to pay profits on that water. As a friend of mine once put it, the greatest need of Canada today is some means of protecting her good business men from her big business men. The good business man improves his methods; the big business man sees the possibility, because of these improved methods, of increasing profits if he can get control of the industry- and he does so. He gets control and then proceeds to find ways and means of keeping prices up, retaining for himself and his associates the advantage of these inventions which should be passed on to the consumer.
In the days of our grandfathers a man could build a flour mill on the side of a stream and grind the people's wheat into

Production-Mr. Bothwell
flour. At that time we had a law which provided that no miller could take more than 20 per cent toll on the grain he ground. A farmer could take 187^ pounds of wheat to the mill and for that receive 100 pounds of flour, 50 pounds of bran and shorts, leaving 37| pounds with the miller as bis toll. And at that rate many millers laid the foundations of substantial fortunes. To-day I live within one hundred miles of one of the most modern mills in the country, and it takes 540 pounds of wheat to buy 100 pounds of their flour, and I get no bran or shorts. That is in one modern up to date mill. Not very far away in another direction a farmer has erected a small mill and he will grind wheat and deliver it in the same town at the rate of 100 pounds for 360 pounds of wheat. This would seem to indicate that the larger the mill the higher the prices they have to charge. I cannot believe that, with these immense mills with all modern machinery and with labour costs reduced to a minimum, it is necessary for them to charge such prices. If i.t is, then I say they are not economical, and I think it would be very interesting for the government to find out exactly why it is that with all these modem inventions and all these improvements in processes of production and in methods of distribution, we find ourselves paying ever higher and higher prices instead of lower prices. I do not think it would be a very expensive thing to get at the facts; it would be merely a matter of gathering of statistics to find out the cost of producing and distributing goods: What are your capital costs? What are your labour costs? What are your selling costs? What do you pay in rent? What do you pay for the lease of land, and so forth? These facts can be easily discovered. Let the information be gathered in the form of statistics and it is not a difficult matter then to interpret them. If we got such information I believe we should find that in many industries we are paying far more than is at all necessary for the products we buy.

speechtext:
This resolution asks for an inquiry under the Research Council Act. There is ample power under that act to inquire into the subject under discussion. Under section 10(c) of the act the council is empowered to undertake in such a way as may be deemed advisable researches with the object of improving the technical processes and methods used in the industries of Canada, and of discovering processes and methods which may promote the expansion of existing or the development of new industries. And under section 10, sub-53719- 118
section (c), paragraph (vii) the council has power to carry out researches, the object of which is to improve conditions in agriculture.
Under both these sections I think there is ample power, and the illustrations given by those hon. members who have spoken before me, as well as the few illustrations I will give, will, I think, impress upon the government the necessity of having an inquiry.
A few days before leaving for Ottawa to attend this session, I saw a demonstration of General Motors in the city of Swift Current. They had three or four different makes of cars there, and one of the representatives of General Motors seemed to think that a Chevrolet car was the kind of car that the farmers in that district should buy. It would represent a price of around $900, a reduction of $400 odd as compared to what it was a few years ago. For that car, priced at $900, the farmer would have to pay 3,600 bushels of wheat, and when that car was selling for $1,300 or thereabouts, 3,600 bushels of wheat would have bought three of them.
In Montreal this past summer harness leather, but not made into harnesses, was worth 40 cents a pound, and at the same time cow skins were worth a cent a pound. Shoes were selling at from $7 to $10 a pair, while calf skins were selling at 10 cents apiece. The hon. member for Assiniboia spoke about wool and the cost of the articles manufactured therefrom. A few days ago there appeared in one of the western papers a letter from a gentleman in the province of Saskatchewan, telling his experience with wool. He was offered from two to three cents a pound for his wool, according to grade, colour and so on. They could not get it much lower than that-it varied from two to three cents. He accepted that price and shipped the wool to a woollen mill in Ontario to have it made into blankets. When he received the blankets he sold them in competition with the stores and realized eighteen cents per pound for his wool, after allowing for freight on the wool from Saskatchewan to Ontario and on the blankets from Ontario to Saskatchewan.
Last summer a farmer went into his home town to get a pair of shafts for his horse rake. He went to the Massey-Harris agency, where he was quoted $4.50. He thought it was too much and said he would go to the planing mill and get them made. The agent offered to order them from the mill for him, but he said he would do it himself. He went to the mill and had the shafts sawn into the right shape, and the completed article cost him $1. He had to drill a couple of holes

Production-Mr. Stevens

before he could use them, but I think this illustrates the great difference there is in the cost of manufacture of certain articles and the retail price. It might be interesting to note that the Massey-Harris agent told him that as they were selling very little new machinery, they had to charge more for the parts.
Another farmer in the same district bought a set of bob-sleighs for which he paid $55. Last winter he thought he would try to make up a set. He took his own timber out of the bush, had it sawn, and made up the sleighs. He bought some bolts and used the shoeing off some old sleighs. His actual outlay was $4.25, his time being put in for nothing. While it may not be just as good a set as he could have bought, they answered the farmer's purposes just about as well as the set for which he had paid $55. The shoeing, not being new, may wear out a little more quickly, but the sleighs are very serviceable. The same farmer needed some doubletrees, and upon pricing them found that they would cost $3. He had them made up at the local mill at a cost of eighty cents, and then used some paint which he happened _ to have around to finish off the article.
With mills and factories properly equipped to manufacture these things, there would seem to be too great a spread between what they charge and what it costs a man to have them made in a rather crude sort of way. These illustrations would1 seem to prove that there is too much difference between the cost of raw material and the price of the finished product. I support the resolution because I believe that valuable work can be done by the research council along these lines.
